speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian men and women who represented Canada so well in the Persian Gulf war will receive their volunteer service medals from the Canadian government on June 22, 1991.
These well-deserved medals will be presented the day before the Canadian Korean Veterans Day celebrations on June 23. This year's celebration will commemorate the 41st anniversary of the Korean war.
When is the Canadian government going to present distinctly Canadian medals to the men and women from every Canadian province and every territory who served voluntarily on behalf of Canada in the Korean war?

Mr. Speaker, this week is National Environment Week across Canada.
I would like to quote from Canada's Green Plan for a healthy environment, which says that although the environment is every individual's responsibility, this responsibility should be reflected in concerted efforts at all levels of society.
National Environment Week emphasizes the partnership concept, and this year more than ever before, groups at every level of our society have joined the government in a nation-wide campaign for commitment and action.
By working together with our partners to make every week environment week, we can build a healthy and prosperous future for this country, Mr. Speaker.
In Quebec and Beauce, people are becoming more and more environment-conscious. This government's efforts are admirable, but every individual must be committed to protecting the environment.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce says that on employment equity the government should first get its own House in order.
The case in point remains Dr. Chander Grover who was fired because he dared to file a complaint of discrimination against the National Research Council.
After dragging out the ordeal to inflict the most damaging psychological and financial punishment possible, the NRC reversed Grover's dismissal when the outcry from the visible minority community became too loud to ignore. However, there was no repentance and no victory because NRC still had many weapons in its bureaucratic armoury.
Grover is now a technician supervised by a boss lacking his international prestige while another less qualified than he does what was Grover's life work.
To challenge this would be insubordination; to accept would be to capitulate to racism.
For the Public Service, that is good enough for government. The Chamber of Commerce has a point.

Mr. Speaker, to millions of people around the world scouting represents a movement which has improved their way of life.

June 5, 1991
Scouting, rooted in the belief in God and in one's own country, teaches young people everywhere to do their best and always be prepared.
As a former Queen's Scout, I am delighted to announce the formation of the Canadian Scout Parliamentary Union, thanks to an initiative which began with our colleagues in Korea, and other Parliaments across this world that have joined together.
I would like to urge my colleagues from both sides of the House to join those founding members from Peterborough, Okanagan Centre, Fraser Valley West and London-Middlesex by stepping forward to assist in the formation of this union.
Some 265,000 Canadians involved in scouting will enjoy and need the support of this Parliament in what is going to happen in the future of scouting in the world.

Mr. Speaker, the environment is important to you and it is important to me. No doubt you would agree that Canadians must be concerned about the environmental and social implications of large energy projects not only in this country, but everywhere in our global community.
One large project currently planned is in Thailand. This project proposes the construction of a hydroelectric dam on the Mun River, the largest tributary of the Mekong River.
The Thai public has demanded by way of petition and personal representation to World Bank officials in its country, that a moratorium be put on this project. The numbers ol people to be displaced and resettled are in dispute. Basic data and analysis by the Electrical Generating Authority of Thailand have not been released, despite repeated requests by villagers, citizen's groups and concerned academics.
Fertile land and fishing will be destroyed. I call on our Minister of Finance, as Canada's Governor to the World Bank, to vote against extending a loan to Thailand for
this project until the public in Thailand has had its concerns met.

For months, ever since the cancellation of the At and East subsidy in 1989, I and my colleagues have been begging the government to help this once great port to survive.
Two weeks ago the Minister of Transport told me that he would see that CN did "what was right". One week ago the minister told me he would do everything in his power to alleviate Halifax's problem.
It took nearly two years to get any response to our questions at all. How much longer must we wait for action?

years ago. It has taken this government a scant seven years to put the port in jeopardy.
Why will the government not act and act now?']

Mr. Speaker, I respectfully request and urge the Standing Committee on House Management review the Question Period process. Canadians are sending a message loud and clear that they want the politicians to change. They are demanding that private members speak out on behalf of their constituents and no longer act in a strict partisan fashion, and that includes during Question Period.
We take pride in the fact that we are a democratic country of equal opportunity and access, but our own House of Commons Question Period is undemocratic and not all MPs enjoy equal opportunity. A minority of members have a better opportunity to represent their constituents than others.
The Canadians I represent deserve the same opportunity to be represented as any other Canadians. Just because I sit on this side of the House does not mean my constituents do not have problems and concerns they want addressed, but it does not mean that I always agree with the government.
As usual, the Canadian people are ahead of the politicians. All I ask the committee to do is to ensure that all members of the House of Commons have an equal opportunity to represent their constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House concerns over the Prime Minister's recent statements regarding compensation for Hong Kong prisoners of war.
Despite the Prime Minister's announcement that Canada extinguished its rights to any further claims to compensation, I wish to draw to the attention of the House, sections 130 and 131 of the Third Geneva Convention which specifically prohibit one government from entering into an agreement with another government that would wilfully deprive its citizens of the rights

to undertake legal action for liability pursuant to the terms of the Geneva Convention.
The Prime Minister's statement is in no way consistent with the tenets of international law or Canada's position on human rights. The Prime Minister should understand that Japan's apology for its violations of the Geneva Convention has only added legitimacy to support the claims of the Hong Kong war veterans of Canada, and that his unfounded statements in regard to the matter have done a great disservice to those veterans who suffered the brutal atrocities of war in the service of their country.

Mr. Speaker, last Sunday, I attended a ceremony to name a municipal park in honour of Mr. Pierre Foumelle, a resident of Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts.
Mr. Foumelle has done volunteer work for 34 years in the riding of Laurentides, mostly in the field of amateur sport. His excellent work and endless dedication are impressive.
The fact that so many sports, including baseball and minor hockey, are popular in our region is largely due to the activities of Mr. Foumelle.
And, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Fournelle's commitment reaches above and beyond the boundaries of the riding of Laurentides, since he is also involved in a number of sports federations at the regional and provincial level.
I want to offer my sincere thanks to Mr. Foumelle for the many years he has dedicated his fellow citizens. He truly deserves to be held in high esteem.

Mr. Speaker, 50,000 Canadians will die from heart attacks this year. Many of them will die suddenly and with family members and friends looking on helplessly. This is an
unnecessary tragedy, given that there are life saving techniques available to all who care to learn them.
CPR teaches one how to recognize heart attack signals and how to perform the technique should a victim's heart stop before an ambulance arrives.

I urge all my colleagues in the House of Commons and the other place to attend the CPR information sessions to be held here on the Hill on Monday, June 10, from 11 a.m to 2 p.m.

I urge all my colleagues to attend the CPR information sessions being held on Parliament Hill on Monday, June 10 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Let us all learn how to save a life.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Customs: A Pivotal Role at the Border headlines the second edition of the crossborder report.
Canada Customs officials, our front line troops, assume a pivotal role in the cross-border shopping puzzle. First, there is the role of protection: protecting our interests through their enforcement and border control activities.
However, Canada Customs are asked to balance security with efficiency, the support of national priorities, the facilitation of trade activities, and the movement of travellers. In particular, what this means is the collection of the applicable duties and taxes from all citizens re-entering Canada with purchases and, at the same time, moving the traffic through the border points.
In the end, all members will agree that Canada cannot afford long line-ups at the border. We are losing valuable American tourist revenue, as well as duty and taxes through wave-throughs.
This may mean more efficient use of technology and current work forces, more personnel, the trial of express lanes, and/or something else.
The objective must be the collection of all applicable duties and taxes in the absence of excessive line-ups at the border.

June 5, 1991
Our Canada Custom officials are a valuable front line force in our efforts to address cross-border traffic volume. We need new initiatives to help them make headway on this matter.
Stay tuned, Mr. Speaker and colleagues, for the next edition of the cross-border report.

Mr. Speaker, today is World Environment Day, a date on the calendar first proclaimed by the United Nations in 1972 and celebrated each subsequent year since on June 5.
World Environment Day not only highlights the many necessary and essential works undertaken by the United Nations in the area of environment but also reminds us that all peoples of the world share a common home and a responsibility for its healthy upkeep.
It is no coincidence that Canadians observe National Environment Week in the same time frame. Not only does our National Environment Week focus on promoting environmental awareness among Canadians and an appreciation of our unique and beautiful country, but it also serves as a vivid reminder that we are all accountable stewards of the earth.
While there is still much work to be done in dealing with the world's serious environmental problems, let us take advantage of World Environment Day and National Environment Week to celebrate what we have accomplished so far and reflect on what we can do in the future to make Canada the most environmentally friendly place on the planet.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday the National Council of Welfare issued a report on the financing of medicare and post-secondary education in Canada. The report did not mince words.
It said that if federal funding cuts were allowed to stand, medicare would be effectively dead as a national health care system. What could be clearer than that statement? Certainly not the Prime Minister's response
that the report was inaccurate and the numbers mentioned were not justified by government projections, and certainly not the Prime Minister's waffling on the introduction of user fees.
The Association of Universities and Colleges in Canada, the Canadian Council on Social Development and the Canadian Medical Association have all stated that medicare is threatened by these unilateral funding cuts which will amount to $62.4 billion by the end of this century.
Canadians are greatly concerned about medicare and its future.
At the provincial health ministers' meeting on June 19 the government must announce two actions: first, the unilateral federal funding cuts to medicare will be reversed and, second, the federal government will ensure that neither user fees nor extra billings will be introduced in any province.

Mr. Speaker, in 1891 in the community of Inglewood, Ontario a public library opened. The Inglewood Mechanics Institute Library that year had 178 volumes and 104 members.
Over the years the number of books grew as the library changed locations from a public hall to a hardware store, to a church, to an ice cream parlour. Today, the library is part of the town of Caledon library system and it gives me great pleasure to rise in my place and salute a hundred years of learning, literature, knowledge and progress in this community in my riding.
It is also an honour to thank a century of people who volunteered their time and energy to see that the printed word in Inglewood, Ontario was treasured and shared.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian Environment Week from June 2 to June 8 is a time for optimism. This is because it involves partnerships among government, industry, environmental groups, labour, health, youth, native groups, church organizations, and many others.
June 5, 1991

Oral Questions
At the community level and at the national level all these partners work toward the common goal of increasing Canada's year-round involvement in safeguarding our environment.
On June 7, the Minister of Environment Canada will be presenting environmental achievement awards that celebrate the effort and commitment of Canadians from all walks of life who work to protect and restore our environment. These groups and individuals remind us of our responsibility to care for our environment, and indeed for our planet. These achievements prove that as individuals and as groups we can make a difference, and the awards that they receive confirm that Canada values the health of its environment.
Let us hope that these award winners will be an inspiration for others to join the environmental team. They symbolize both our national commitment to a sustainable environment and the esteem in which this nation holds those Canadians who lead us toward achieving that commitment.
I also want to mention the thousands of other unsung heroes and heroines-
I am afraid the hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, once again I rise in this House to plead for assistance to the port of Halifax.
For months, ever since the cancellation of the At and East subsidy in 1989, I and my colleagues have been begging the government to help this once great port to survive.
Two weeks ago the Minister of Transport told me that he would see that CN did "what was right". One week ago the minister told me he would do everything in his power to alleviate Halifax's problem.
It took nearly two years to get any response to our questions at all. How much longer must we wait for action?
Essentially the problems for the port are twofold: uncompetitive freight rates and an unfair tax structure. Halifax had been a thriving port since its founding 242
years ago. It has taken this government a scant seven years to put the port in jeopardy.
Why will the government not act and act now?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
For a number of years now we have been discussing in the Arctic the infringement on Canadian territory by the United States in terms of issuing oil and gas drilling leases on Canadian territory.
Once again, this year, May 20, 1991, the Department of the Interior says that under sale 124, it is going to issue oil and gas drilling licences in the Beaufort Sea in Canadian territory.
Just four years ago. in 1987, this same issue arose. What has this government done in four years to establish Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic north?

This will mean that the 200,000 Porcupine caribou herd will be jeopardized for 200 days of oil, as will the lives of the Gwitch'in people of Yukon and Alaska.
I ask the Prime Minister: Is he willing to intervene directly to protect Canadian sovereignty in this issue, to speak to President Bush and say this is unacceptable to Canada, to have drilling in ANWR, and it is unacceptable to Canada for the United States to sell off bits of Canada piece by piece?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the hon. House leader of the New Democratic Party reading Beauchesne's concerning Question Period. I hope he reads it all and counsels his members accordingly in terms of what is a proper question and what is not.
Clearly, one of the citations state that questions should not be repeated. I was simply making the point that it was a repetition of the question and I repeated the answer. The answer was "yes" as it was the previous time it was asked.
Mr. Speaker, your comments in terms of the other two points of order are appropriate and I agree with those comments. I think they need to be looked into.
I would just like to, very briefly, make a couple of points. One concerns what constitutes a question. Citation 411(2) in Beauchesne's sixth edition says:
A question may not:
(2)	seek information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as decisions of proceedings of Cabinet -
Discussions between cabinet ministers are by their nature secret and discussions between ministers and officials are by their nature secret. I think it is in keeping with the citation to suggest that those questions ought not to be asked. Mr. Speaker, you can appreciate the difficulty it creates if members are going to stand up and ask: "Now what did you discuss with your colleagues at this meeting and that meeting and so on?" They are by their nature secret, as are formal cabinet meetings. However, any time one of my colleagues discusses matters within our administrative responsibility, we are discussing matters which are by their nature secret and ought not to be questions, according to Beauchesne's- which, I repeat, should be enforced.
As for the question of whether the proceedings of a committee should be a matter for questions in the House, raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kings-way on a point of order, 411(3) says:
A question may not:
(3)	seek information about proceedings in a committee which has not yet made its report to the House.
The reason for that citation should obviously be clear. This matter is fairly complex. There are a number of documents and people involved and so on. In committee the complexity can be explored. At the end of the day, when all the information has been deduced before committee, conclusions can be reached. That is the appropriate forum. To extract out of context one or two items to bring forward to the House is certainly not to serve the purposes of elucidation and clarity for the benefit of the public, but rather to serve other purposes.
In that context, that is a very good explanation of why this citation is in Beauchesne's and why it was entirely appropriate that the citation be enforced in this instance. Members should not use this forum as a mechanism for extracting from the committee those items they find to be to their partisan advantage to be brought forward in the House.
I do not think that serves the public purpose or the public's ability to know the true situation or the facts. It is also not in keeping with what Question Period is supposed to be, namely the opportunity for the opposition to seek information that cannot be obtained in other more appropriate mechanisms such as letter writing, proceedings in committee and so on.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the points of order which have been raised by both my colleague from Burnaby and the government House leader.
The government House leader suggested to the House that when cabinet ministers have discussions, by their very nature they are secret. That, in my view, is somewhat absurd.
There is a big distinction to be made between cabinet ministers meeting and discussing certain points and a cabinet meeting being struck for the purposes of making the decision.
At a cabinet meeting there is a secretary, there are minutes and there are copies of the decisions that have been reached at that particular meeting.
To suggest to the House that each and every conversation between two cabinet ministers, whatever it may be, is somehow sacred is absolutely absurd and I believe should not be found by the Chair or by anyone to be an appropriate point of order.
June 5, 1991

Second, with regard to the point of order raised by my colleague from Burnaby concerning proceedings at committee not being allowed to be raised on the floor of the House of Commons for Question Period, Mr. Speaker, you have given an undertaking to that member and I believe through him to the House that you will reflect on the "blues".
I would simply ask you, Mr. Speaker, prior to making any adjudication to give due notice to the various political parties so that we will have an opportunity to make additional representations to you. While you are reflecting on that, let us draw the distinction that the hon. member has made.
I am looking at the fifth edition of Beauchesne's. My sixth edition is not with me today, but I am sure members will bear with me.
I refer to paragraph 360(3) which talks about seeking information about proceedings in a committee which has not yet made its report to the House.
Let us be very clear. The wording says: "proceedings". It does not say: "subject matter". There is quite a distinction to be made between proceedings on one hand and subject matter on the other.
My second point is the following. We have in the rules in Beauchesne's a rule which has been tradition through the years, which I know my colleague in the New Democratic Party and the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader will probably want to speak to if not today, later in the debate. That is the sub judice rule.
That specifically refers to subject matter before a court. It says: "subject matter".
This citation concerns proceedings. It does not concern subject matter. If it was to have been subject matter, the rule would have been clear. It would have been spelled out that subject matter is not to be raised on the floor in Question Period.
Finally, it must be understood-the Chair is well aware of this and I am sure the Table is also-that there are numerous agencies of the Government of Canada which are obligated by statute to file statutory reports to various standing committees of the House of Commons.
Today, we have some 40 federal departments, 40 different ministries and there are numerous reports that
Point of Order
are filed with the Clerk and are automatically referred. There is no debate. They are automatically referred to standing committees. Is the Chair going to say to members of Parliament that because that subject matter has been referred to a standing committee that this particular body has no right, no authority whatsoever to examine the subject matter and to raise questions? It is absolutely absurd to suggest that.
Finally, in terms of the distinction, standing committees of the House are not independent, quasi or judicial bodies of the House. They are creatures of the House. It is Parliament, I suggest, through the Chair to hon. members, that is the final authority, and you, Mr. Speaker, the final arbitrator in terms of what is acceptable or not acceptable.
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will reflect on those comments. But I wish to make the caveat, that before any adjudication is made with regard to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Burnaby that all members-myself, my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier, my colleague from Kingston and the Islands, and I am sure more members-would want to have the opportunity to make interventions.
I make those general comments for the Chair so that the Chair might reflect on the absurdity that is being promoted by the government House leader with regard to that point of order; and, second, his point of order that cabinet ministers when they meet on the street and talk, their conversations somehow are secret, is absolutely and unequivocally nonsense.

Just on a very short point of order to complement the point being made by my hon. friend, the House leader for the Official Opposition.

The meaning of the term 'proceedings' in Parliament: The primary
meaning, as a technical parliamentary term of proceedings, is some

I think the whole thrust of that is to say that the reason we don't have a committee hearing and then an hour or two later the same issue heard a second time in the House of Commons is, as the House leader pointed out earlier, that we would be taking the same issue into two completely different forums, one where you have the
opportunity to explore in detail and have rebuttal. The other is where there is simply to be a quick question and a quick answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: PROCEEDS OF CRIME (MONEY LAUNDERING) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
moved that Bill C-9, an act to facilitate combating the laundering of proceeds of crime, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill we have before us, Bill C-9, entitled an act to facilitate combating the laundering of proceeds of crime, is part of Canada's national drug strategy. As such, it builds on and complements
June 5, 1991

other legislation that Canada has introduced in this area, most notably Bill C-58 which was designed to enhance international law enforcement co-operation and Bill C-61 which made money laundering a criminal offence.
Its purpose is to discourage the use of Canada's financial system by criminals and to ensure that there is an adequate paper trail for our law enforcement authorities to carry out money laundering investigations.
The bill is consistent with the recommendations of the G-7 financial action task force on money laundering and consistent with those of the advisory committee on money laundering, a joint, private-public sector group which I chair.
The bill also has the support of Canada's financial community and a cross-section of senior officials from that community are members of the advisory committee.
Before I turn briefly to the specific measures in the bill, I would like to outline the setting in which the bill was developed.
As you know, drug trafficking, unfortunately, is something which plagues all modern societies. Familiarity, however, should not breed complacency. The destruction that drug trafficking renders is a tragedy of gigantic proportion. Individual lives, families and communities can and are being destroyed in Canada and elsewhere.
Drug trafficking generates large volumes of cash and therein lies both its attraction and its vulnerability. The proceeds of crime, particularly from drug trafficking, must be converted in other seemingly legitimate forms. The act of doing so is of course called "money laundering".
Without money laundering, drug trafficking would be less profitable and, therefore, less attractive to the criminal element in society.

In July 1989, the leaders of the G-7 countries announced the establishment of a Financial Action Task Force to study and make recommendations on measures to combat money laundering. The Task Force's first report was released in April, 1990. It contains 40 recommendations for action. At the Economic Summit in Houston in July 1990 the Prime Minister and the other G-7 leaders made clear their intention to fully implement the Task Force's recommendations quickly.
Government Orders
I think that we all can feel some measure of satisfaction in that Canada is in substantial compliance with the Task Force's recommendations. One area where we fall short, however, is in ensuring that our financial institutions, other businesses and professionals who handle large volumes of cash maintain adequate records. This brings me back to Bill C-9, which is designed to fill this
gap-
The bill, the short title of which is the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) Act, is linked to the criminal offence of money laundering as defined in the Criminal Code, the Narcotics Control Act and the Food and Drug Act.
It is important to note that the provisions of the legislation focus on record keeping, not on reporting. The specific details relating to the keeping of records will be established by regulation. The records in question are limited to those which have been determined to be useful in the prevention, investigation and prosecution of money laundering.
This approach allows us to be flexible so that as the channels by which money is laundered change, the methods used to combat it can be adjusted. The bill is similar in most respects, Mr. Speaker, to Bill C-89, which we introduced in the last Parliament. However, the current bill calls for a consultation period of at least 90 days between the time of publication of regulations issued under the bill and their finalization.
In addition, the wording of certain sections of the bill has been made more precise. The revised bill makes it clear that intent is required before penalties apply. In addition, the regulation-making power of the government, with regard to determining the accuracy of information contained in records, only applies to the identification of clients.
The bill, I can assure you, will not reduce the traditional safeguards with respect to access to these records.
Finally, the bill imposes penalties in accordance with the seriousness of the situation. In closing, I do not need to remind the House that drug trafficking and money laundering pose major challenges to society.

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
Bill C-9 is an important bill for Canadians. It is designed to strike at these social ills but in a way which is not intrusive. It is in the interests of all of us to ensure that Canada does not become a haven for money launderers. I would welcome your support for this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak on this particular bill, Bill C-9, otherwise known as the money laundering bill.
Bill C-9 appeared in the last session as Bill C-89 and it was lost when the House was prorogued. It is probably a good thing that it was because there were some flaws in that particular legislation. We are very pleased to see that the government has responded and made some changes in the legislation that make it a little more workable.
It seems to us that there are still a few things we should take a look at. We understand that everyone is in agreement that this bill be sent off to committee, and that is positive.
The drug war, as we hear it called from time to time, is a major problem in the world. There is absolutely no question about that. Canada has in part been considered a bit of a haven as far as the drug situation is concerned. Because of our close proximity to major drug routes, because we border on the United States and in part because we have lax financial reporting laws, Canada is one of the areas in which we see the drug trade moving. I know I can speak with some knowledge as far as New Brunswick is concerned.
There have been a number of cases where planes containing large amounts of drugs have landed on rural runways. Also, certain people have arrived in the New Brunswick area and deposited guns and everything else to try to free some of the people who have already been incarcerated by our efficient police force.
We know there is a drug problem in New Brunswick. We know there is a drug problem in Canada and this bill will help, in part, to solve the problem. Obviously, the problem has to be attacked on many levels. It has to be attacked where the drugs are being produced. It also has to be attacked at the means of delivery. Third, the criminals who are making a profit on the sale of drugs have to be attacked. I think, in large measure too, consumption also has to be attacked.
There is no question that this particular bill is aimed at one aspect. That is the profits which are associated with drugs and how those get into our community and become legitimate.
The bill builds on the so-called freeze and seize legislation, C-61, which in effect created the offence of money laundering. Money laundering is described as a process by which illegitimate dollars are transformed through the financial markets into legitimate funds. The purpose is to hide the identity of the real owners of the funds and give them the appearance of being legitimate.

There is no question that there is a problem and it is a world-wide problem. The question is whether this legislation goes far enough. We support the bill being considered in committee, but we hope that it will be improved upon thereafter.

There is no question that it is an international problem, and that is really what has forced this matter on this House. It is the United States and the G-7 which have said that all of the nations facing this problem have to become involved. This legislation when it was first presented had to be returned to the drawing boards because it did reflect an American slant. Their laws, as they deal with barristers, solicitors and other professionals, are different than ours so it was necessary for some of the legislation to be redrafted.
The other thing we have to look at is the area of regulation. A lot of this particular legislation is aimed at allowing the law to really develop through regulation. In some senses that is good but in others it is bad because the regulations do not have the control that Parliament has over intrusions into peoples' lives. We have to remember that is the effect of this legislation.
Any transaction over $10,000 is going to be subject to an intrusion by government, in effect through the reporting of those transactions in financial institutions. On the face of it that is good. There is no question, that is the only way we are going to track this situation. At the same time, it is an intrusion into peoples' lives and we have to make sure there is a balance and that we are going to benefit.
June 5, 1991

There is no assurance yet, nor have we seen any of the necessary money placed on the table to ensure it, that the government, the RCMP and the crime enforcement agencies are going to use this information. We have to be assured that when the information is sent from the financial institutions to the law enforcement agencies that they are going to have the resources and people and the money, all of the things that are necessary, to ensure that something good will come from this legislation. It does no one any good for this information to end up on a shelf in some RCMP office without being utilized. Therefore, that becomes a major concern.
As well, with respect to the regulations, there is a concern among many that the regulations will be proclaimed, and that the different professions and different institutions which are affected will not be fully aware and not have the input that they would have if it was an actual bill that came through Parliament.
We are hopeful that in the long run there will be more control over the regulations so that the adverse effects of regulations which slip through will not be felt. We are pleased that the government at least is going to have a three-month consultation process prior to the regulations coming into effect.
There is also protection for lawyers, as far as solicitor-client privilege is concerned, as that is the other problem and is where we differ a little bit from the American system. Lawyers were faced with the conundrum of not being able to divulge information given to them by their client while, at the same time, having to face a penalty for not giving out that information. There is an attempt to clean up that particular problem.
We also see that the government is going to define "cash" and say what that term really means. That is a loose end that certain criminal elements could hide behind.
The other broad aspect of this bill is that we are going to see an attempt to close some of the borders as far as Canada is concerned. One of the mechanisms to be closed is using Canada's financial system to legitimize illegitimate money.
Government Orders
However, the critical aspect and something that will become interesting once the committee meets is how effective the other countries are going to be. If we do not have connections between all of the other countries then it is not going to work. The other thing we have to be aware of is that the information gathered on Canadians will be available to other countries and other law enforcement agencies. That is a good point and a bad point, as it is an intrusion into the privacy of Canadians. We have to do a cost benefit analysis to ensure that there are not adverse effects on Canadians.
The Liberal Party is prepared to support this bill at this particular stage. We are excited that it will go to committee and that we will have before us all the different interest groups involved, such as the bar society and the bankers' society. We do not know which committee, but it will be one of the very important committees of this House I am sure, perhaps the one which the hon. member chairs.
In any event, the fact that it goes to committee and that we can have submissions from those different interest groups is important. In addition to the involvement of the barristers, the chartered accountants and the bankers' associations, a good idea that has been suggested-perhaps by the chairman of that committee-is that the RCMP be involved in advising us as to what the status of things is.
Second, it probably would not hurt for us to have someone from one of the civil liberties organizations appear to talk about the cost benefits of these intrusions. Let it be perfectly clear that the Liberal Party is fully supportive of the efforts to fight the drug situation in our country and on our streets. We are prepared to go to most levels in order to have legislation which will assist law enforcement agencies in achieving that goal. However, we are not prepared to go to the extent of a complete denial of civil liberties and individual Canadians' rights.
That is why this committee is important. That is why we want to see it at committee. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the time to give comments on this particular bill.

speechtext:
Occasionally there is a piece of legislation which comes before the House and receives the unanimous support of all parties, and which has reached the House through a process of negotiation and discussion, which helps to explain that

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
unanimous support. In the case of this piece of legislation, that is very much the reality.
This legislation is a result of the decisions of the G-7 countries to, quite rightly, attempt to ensure that what we assume to be tremendous monetaiy flows taking place as a consequence of the illicit drug trade are made easier to track and easier to police. As my colleagues in the Liberal Party have suggested this is not for purposes of trying, to somehow hurt the privacy of people, but instead of suggesting ways for our financial institutions in this country to help control more effectively this large scale flow of illicit funds.
We are talking about the flow of illicit funds which is especially important to track. If it is not possible to do so then these illicit funds become the basis on which legal activities are established within this country. This in turn permits further profit making on the basis of what was originally an illicit sale of drugs with subsequent flow of illicit money.
From our perspective as a party we strongly share the basic purposes and goals which lie behind this legislation, and that is to try to see to it that the flow of illicit funds does not become possible in our country. It is not a secret that Canada has been seen as a relatively easy country through which money laundering can take place. This is not a reputation that any of us in this House would want this country to have, and I am certain everybody in the House will support tightening up the situation.
Our concerns however with the original bill, which came before us in a previous session of this Parliament, were that in the process of attempting to deal with a serious problem the government had established a number of clauses as part of the legislation, a number of regulations as part of the draft regulations prepared to support the legislation which frankly represented certain dangers. These dangers could conceivably penetrate for instance the relationship between a lawyer and a lawyer's clients. That penetration could begin through the search for a monetary trail based on money exchanges, but it would have the effect of leading from the purely financial considerations involved into a detailed probing, we feared and the Canadian Bar Association feared, of the lawyer-client relationship which existed in a number of situations.
It is for that reason that the original version of this legislation was very strongly condemned by the Canadian Bar Association.
The Canadian Bar Association is not an organization which ordinarily takes strong positions on pieces of federal government legislation. Yet, the Canadian Bar Association did take the highly unusual step of passing a motion at the national level, condemning this piece of legislation as it was originally drafted.
We talked about this piece of legislation with members from the opposite side, the government side. They assured us that at the time the previous legislation was in front of us, there were no problems.
We however checked to see if this were the case with a number of associations such as the Canadian Bar Association. It indicated to us that unfortunately, contrary to what we have been told, there were serious problems which led them to pass this national resolution.
Subsequently, we indicated that we would not be prepared to co-operate with the passage of this legislation. It was after this, as I understand it, that the government finally entered into serious discussion with the Canadian Bar Association and came to conclusions which now resolve the problems that were in the previous piece of legislation.
We have discussed the new piece of legislation with the Canadian Bar Association. We have discussed it with the body that represents the Canadian Chartered Accountants. We are assured by both that they see no problems with the bill as it presently stands.
We have talked with representatives of the chartered banks who have also indicated that there should be no problem from their perspective with the period of time for which financial records are required to be kept under the legislation.
I think, as a consequence of further consultation, we have a much better piece of legislation in front of us now than we had in the previous session of Parliament.
For this reason we are prepared as a party to support the legislation because, as I say, we strongly agree with the principle. Our concern was with some of the details.
June 5, 1991

Those details have now been worked through with some of the bodies that previously expressed concern.
We would still hope that when this bill goes to committee, whether it is a legislative committee or a specific standing committee, it will call before it some of those organizations which expressed concern in the past so that those concerns will in fact be overcome by the changes which have taken place.
We have heard from such organizations. We take their word, but I think it is important to see that this is explored at committee.
I have had some discussions with the parliamentary secretary to the minister. I think there is widespread agreement with respect to the three or four groups that we would want to see come before the committee.
I hope that speedy passage through the committee will therefore be assured. I am pleased to say that as far as we are concerned, we are very pleased to see speedy passage at second reading of a significant piece of legislation.
It will not in any sense be a comprehensive response, but it will be a significant part of the response to try to deal with the illicit flow of funds associated with the drug trade in our country.

The House resumed from Thursday, May 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-6, an act respecting the exporting, importing, manufacturing, buying or selling of or other dealing with certain weapons be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this legislation with a great deal of mixed
Government Orders
feelings. Canada has had a history of being a nation which, on the whole, has worked for peace. It has been in the forefront of attempting to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons and to provide peacekeeping forces within the United Nations.
Within my own family there is a long and strong tradition of working for peace. My father grew up in Russia belonging to a group called the Molokans, whose members are much like the Quakers; pacifists. He was fortunate enough to be able to leave Russia when he became draft age and he chose to come to Canada because he knew that Canada allowed for religious and political freedom. He was involved in some of the first peace movements in Canada including, I am proud to say, leading some of the first demonstrations and marches against the bomb in 1946 and 1947.
He spoke about many things in the late forties and early fifties and at that time, particularly if you had a Russian name, it was not easy to stand up and advocate peace initiatives. Many years later, when it became more acceptable, many of the things that he suggested, the total community adopted and realized that they only made sense in a modem society.
What we have here is the start of a new government initiative to get Canada farther into the area of arms sales. It is one of these things that becomes a treadmill. The farther you get into it, the more difficult it is to get out.
It is based on a number of very shaky premises. Under the present export control policy, Canada has agreed to a number of things. I think it is worth while looking at what they are. Basically Canada agreed to four things: it would not export military goods to countries that pose a threat to Canada or its allies; it would not export military goods to countries that are involved in or under imminent threat of hostility; it would not export military goods to countries under United Nations Security Council sanctions; it would not export military goods to countries whose governments have a persistent record of serious violation of human rights of their citizens.
Some of the current proposals would fail on two of these grounds. The current proposals are designed to start and dump back military armaments into the mideast, including Saudi Arabia. If anyone looks at the history of the mid-east in the last four years, or 10 years,

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
it would be very difficult to say who are our allies are and who are our enemies.
We have decided at various times that Iran is our enemy. During the war, maybe Iran was our ally. We armed Iraq because we decided Iraq was our ally when it was involved in the war with Iran. Where do nations like Syria, Saudi Arabia, some of the other gulf states and even Kuwait stand?
Certainly neither Saudi Arabia nor Kuwait would stand the last test of countries whose governments have a persistent record of serious violations of human rights of their citizens and yet we are prepared to start re-arming undemocratic regimes.
There are many other mid-east countries that I get very concerned about, such as United Arab Emerates in which I had the pleasure of spending two weeks. At this point it is a peaceful country. It is under no threat internally or from any of its neighbours, but it is ruled by one family and one family only, with no pretence of democracy or freedom and with dictatorial policies along religious lines. Yet I see this morning that the United States has just decided to sell it 12 military attack helicopters and 6 to Bahrain.
What are they going to do with those? One becomes suspicious as there is a new birth of democracy sweeping through some of these countries, making sure that they have the means of ensuring their own continued survival.
The whole experience within the war in the gulf should have taught us something. It should have taught us that Iraq would have been militarily incapable of violating the sovereignty of its fellow nations. It would have been militarily incapable of perpetuating the war with its mass destruction. Hussein would have not been able to maintain his dictatorship had it not been for the arms supplied to him and Iraq by the five permanent members of the UN Security Council; Britain, France, China, U.S.S.R and the United States.
It seems to me that Canada was involved in testing weapons that ended up in Iraq. Now we want to get involved in the actual sale of arms to countries that are involved in conflict and in violation of civil rights.
All this does is detract dramatically from Canada's ability to be a peace negotiator in this world. Our whole
credibility as a peacekeeping nation and a peace negotiator was trampled on dramatically during the gulf war.
We rushed in and backed the United States in a military operation that turned out to be an environmental disaster with a huge loss of life. At least 100,000,
150,000	or 200,000 people died in that war.
The Kurds have been totally disrupted. The environment in the gulf has been totally wiped out for 50 or 100 years, or maybe forever. Canada blindly went along.
Now we have the government saying that for the sake of a few jobs we will sacrifice another piece of our prestige, integrity, neutrality, and our ability to act as a peace negotiator and peacekeeper in this world. We will do so being blind to the history since the Second World War. If there were somebody on Mars to look down at us, they would ask: "What is this race of creatures down there doing? It looks like a football scrum has picked up and that they change sides evety weekend and have another go at it".
Our strong ally right now is Japan. It was our enemy less than 40 years ago. Less than five years ago, our worst enemy was the Soviet Union. Now it is considered our ally.
We have even been involved in conflicts in the mideast on both sides of the argument and in other areas. Think back to the Falklands war between Argentina and Britain in which the British were being fired upon by French weapons.
We always make the assumption that we know who our friends are, our loyal friends. Particularly in the mid-east the situation is volatile. No one can guarantee that countries which pose a threat to Canada or to its allies are countries that are involved in or are under imminent threat of hostilities. All of those countries are involved in an ongoing regional war in which the western and Soviet bloc powers have armed them in order to escalate arms sales.
Military spending in this world is out of control. It is $1,000 billion a year, $1,000 billion a year. That is a figure that is totally incomprehensible to most Canadians and to most people in this world. Yet we persist. This bill does not say: "Look, we want to see military spending in the world go down so that it can be directed to positive uses". It simply says: "We want a piece of the pie".
June 5, 1991

We want to be able to say that there is this military spending and we want to get in on the action because it is good for business and profit making.
It is funny how very quickly people's attitudes change. When the gulf war was at its height, we heard from the government some very encouraging speeches. For a moment, I was almost proud of a government that was speaking on my behalf.
T he minister of external affairs spoke out clearly saying: "The world cannot let a victory become a truce, an occasion for nations to rearm, to regroup and return to battle". That was a statement that clearly said we have to put an end to this type of arms trade.
The Prime Minister made very, very high sounding statements. He talked about the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the arms trade and the constant chasing of spheres of influence. He said: "We could be big arms merchants. We chose not to be, although it is a veiy lucrative business. We chose not to be, because it is fundamentally inconsistent with our policy to develop it, to peddle it, to finance it and then to deplore its use".
If only the Prime Minister really believed what he was saying at that time, if only he had been willing to commit his government to that type of policy and to say: "Not only have we chosen not to, we will not be involved in developing it. We will not be involved in peddling it. We will not be involved in financing it". All we have left, I guess, is that we will be deploring the use of arms when they start again.
The government tries to indicate that in this time of recession we cannot afford to miss an opportunity for a few jobs. I say to the members on the government side, this is like saying we will keep capital punishment because it makes work for the hangman.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: You are calling the CAW workers hangmen. That is what you are doing.

I am saying that the government is so short-sighted that it cannot look at anything but the employment advantages. It has no ability to say: "Look, we have a moral obligation to the men and women in those factories to find them alternative employment. To shut them down today and find positive, alternative types of employment".
This government has done such a flip-flop. Where are the statements that the Prime Minister made less than three or four months ago, when he said: "We could be big arms merchants. We chose not to"? Now it is choosing to be when he says: "It is fundamentally inconsistent". Well, now the government has chosen to be inconsistent.
It is almost pathetic that this is one of the first bills to be brought before the House in this new session. What does that say about Canada and Canada's priorities?
We talk about economies and military spending. One begins to wonder whether the economic success of West Germany and Japan was not based in large part on the fact that after World War II, they were in no position to plough their financial resources into rearmament. Instead, they ploughed them into industrial development. They ploughed them into human resources, technology, education and training. I think that is a lesson the rest of the countries, particularly Canada, should learn.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to add my voice to those across this House who are scratching their heads at this moment and asking themselves why the government has chosen this moment, in a very fragile period, just after we have been embroiled in a situation of war in the Persian Gulf, to introduce legislation which sends a confusing and contradictory message to the international community.
Specifically, the confusion revolves around the fact that at the height of the hostilities, the Prime Minister of Canada made great efforts and great pains to suggest that in the post-war period Canada should take charge and be a leader in the area of arms reduction. He made a statement in February in which he said: "Left to proliferate, arms seriously threaten peace around the world". He also said, in a number of post-war initiatives: "This

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
problem must be brought under control and the time to act is now". In fact, he offered to host an international summit aimed at curbing the world arms trade.
We know the difficulty Canada's reputation suffered, specifically as a result of our involvement in hostilities which left us abandoning our historical role as a peacekeeper. But we believed that the initiatives announced by the Prime Minister were a possible ray of hope in a world that clings to the idea that we have in fact embraced a new world order.
However, with the specifics of this legislation and contrary to the position taken by the New Democratic Party, we believe that there is a place in legislation for export and import control. In fact, for many years we have called for specific legislation to permit the arms business, which has existed for many decades in Canada, to be a matter of the public record.
As the Speaker will now know, most exporting of arms is carried out by Order in Council and very specific legislation directed toward friendly countries could be a benefit because it would lay bare the facts surrounding Canada's role in the arms race.
Most people who have involved themselves in the issue of arms control were not surprised to discover, during the height of the Persian Gulf hostilities, that mercenary activity such as gun running and illegally supplying arms, for example to Iraq, was carried on through Canada. We were not surprised either to realize that the arms, in large measure, that were subsequently used to attack the forces of the United Nations were sold to Iraq legitimately by countries in the United Nations, and most specifically by the United States.
While it is true that the elements of the military equation are constantly changing and very fluid, in this party we do believe that a very specific law governing the publication of export orders would be, in effect, a positive step in terms of exposing and highlighting just where we are going on the issue of arms control.
However, we are most concerned that the specifics of this legislation will lead to a wide open sale of arms to countries that are not on the list of friendly countries. I refer specifically to the legislation as presented to the House by the Minister for International Trade in which
he spoke about the role played by the Governor in Council in terms of establishing a list of countries. We feel that this is key to the debate. He says: "According to the legislation, the Governor in Council may establish a list of countries to be called an automatic firearms country control list, including therein any country with which Canada has an intergovernmental defence, research, development and production arrangement".
However, Mr. Speaker, the word "may", as you know, is not an exclusive but rather a general wording which would in fact permit the Governor in Council to extend the list to countries beyond those which are considered friendly countries to Canada.
We know, for example, that one of the specific contracts which this particular piece of legislation was allegedly introduced to support was the sale to Saudi Arabia. We also know that notwithstanding the elements of progress we saw in the relationship as the Persian Gulf events unfolded, Saudi Arabia is still at war with the State of Israel. Saudi Arabia has not denounced the state of war with Israel and, as such, certainly is not one of the countries which would legitimately be included on the list of countries which the Governor in Council is called upon to establish by way of this legislation.
Unlike the NDP, which basically has taken the position that all current arms activity in Canada should be banned forthwith and for which it has absolutely no support in the union movement, we do not believe as a party that we can move as of this date to ban the sale of all arms, in particular to countries which are using those arms in a supportive and a defensive role.
However, we believe that the sale of arms should be public by way of very specific legislation and that the control order should be veiy tight. It should not be left up to the Governor in Council by way of regulation to play with the list as he or she sees fit.
In that context, what we are proposing are some very specific amendments which would in fact tighten the legislation to make it very clear that countries like Saudi Arabia would not be the legitimate recipients of defensive arms from Canada.

An argument was put forward by the Minister for International Trade. He argued here in this House that his particular government was not abandoning its role of arms reduction because in fact the weapons it was talking about were not weapons of mass destruction. You can be killed singly or you can be killed collectively. If you are dead you have still been hit by a weapon of destruction.
I dare say the Canadian public finds that argument rather weak, recognizing that it is the intention of the minister to basically liberalize an activity which has gone on for very many years in Canada but which clearly should be in the sunset and not the sunrise of its activity.
We agree that the Canadian economy over the next decade should not be dependent upon growth from the defence industry. But we also recognize that in the current world order we have not reached the stage of peace and stability where no arms are needed anywhere. In that context, we want to see very specific, well articulated, thoughtful legislation which lays out in the Parliament of Canada just who can receive arms from our country. That is clearly not present in this particular legislation.
Clearly the proposal of the Minister for International Trade that he is only talking about small weapons and not weapons of mass destruction, and the contradictory comments of the Prime Minister that he wants to see Canada as a country that will be leading the way in terms of arms control, simply do not come together.
[Translation\
The public perception is that this is a confusing policy, because, at one time, toward the end of the Persian Gulf war in February, the Prime Minister himself announced a peace plan in which he said he was prepared to preside over a disarmament summit aimed specifically at encouraging arms reduction in the Middle East. However, this legislation, as it stands, does exactly the opposite.
We suggest, Mr. Speaker, that with the proposal put forward by the Minister for International Trade, arms could even be sold directly to Saudi Arabia while it is still at war with the State of Israel.
The problem is that you cannot claim to want arms reduction while, at the same time, introducing a bill liberalizing our capacity to sell arms to any country.

Some Canadians were shocked to hear that the arms used to kill great numbers of people, including allied troops in the coalition, had indeed been sold to Iraq by the United States and other UN member countries when Iraq was at war with Iran, our alleged enemy.
We saw how quickly things changed, Mr. Speaker. That is why we are calling, first of all, for very specific legislation. It is important that exporting of arms be not carried out by a mere Order in Council, as it has been the practice for many years. At the same time, the legislation should be very specific as to which countries should be listed on the Control List and those that should not.
We know that, notwithstanding the NDP policy to the effect that no arms are sold in Canada, arms sales do take place in Canada. We have been selling arms for years. One thing is sure, if we are planning to introduce a disarmament policy, the first thing to do is to find alternate jobs for the workers in that industry.
We also know, Mr. Speaker, that the situation in the Middle East is still volatile and, with the China's policy setback reflected in the Tiananmen Square massacre, the new world order is not quite established.
Earlier, my hon. colleague from the NDP referred to Canada's neutrality. We are not a neutral country. As a member of an alliance, we share certain defensive responsibilities, not offensive ones, Mr. Speaker. But how are we to be expected to defend ourselves if we cannot even arm ourselves? So we do not understand the somewhat hypocritical position taken by the New Democratic Party, by those people who walk around union halls and say they are working for the unions. However, when they come here-and as far as I can see, there have not been a lot of members from Ontario who spoke to this issue-they certainly don't show a lot of courage when we discuss these issues.
Mr. Speaker, I am from Ontario-you may have forgotten that-but I am from an area where steel is the main industry. I am certainly not ashamed to say we want a clear policy, because this one is not clear. It is confusing, and it sends the wrong message to Canadians. We also want some specific amendments concerning the lists, those so-called lists drawn up by the minister. We do not want Canada to be able to sell arms to countries that are still at war with our allies.

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
That is why we intend to propose some specific amendments. We are going to do what we have to do, and one thing is certain: the bill as drafted could never be supported by the Liberal Party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the subject of Saudi Arabia and Israel, does the hon. member realize that when it comes to the light armoured vehicle implication of this export permit act, these are wheeled vehicles and therefore they could not be carried over the desert and therefore they are only defensive weapons with regard to Israel?
Is the hon. member aware that the member for London East, in whose riding the LAV plant is situated, very much supports this bill? Is the hon. member aware of those two points?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware of the position of the member for London East who certainly has been most vocal on this particular issue. I am also aware that obviously the minister requires certain changes of legislation to facilitate this sale. Otherwise we would not be having this discussion in the House. If there is no problem with the sale of the armoured vehicles with wheels as they now exist, obviously there would be no need to be here in the House. There is a problem and we do not want to see a control order list including sale of arms by way of a vehicle where the gun will in fact be put on in another country.
We do not want to see the sale of arms to countries that are currently not on the acceptable list, because that sets the stage for the kind of situation we saw in Iraq, where the Canadian government, and other governments, saw our own allies being attacked by weapons which were sold to the Iraqis by the Americans and other allies. It was a ridiculous situation that left Canadians scratching their heads.
That is why we want to bring to bear amendments which will very specifically deal with who is on the control order list and why and ensure that that will be available public information.

Mr. Speaker, in my brief time here I have found that when the hon. member for Hamilton East begins to accuse the New Democratic
Party of hypocrisy, quite often it is by way of mirror reflection.
I would like to investigate that just briefly, if I may, with specific regard to one of the most potent weapons of destruction in the Iran-Iraq war, the Cruise missile used in Baghdad and other major centres in the festival of the slaughter of the innocents in which we engaged.
Most Canadians will recall that the guidance system of the Cruise missile was manufactured and designed by Litton Industries, a subsidiary of an American parent, in Toronto, Ontario, and was done with the active approval of the former Liberal government of the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. The testing-at least the beginning of the testing-of that same guidance system over Canadian territory was also approved enthusiastically by the Liberal government of Pierre Elliot Trudeau.
I would just like to ask the hon. member if-
No lover's quarrel.

Oh, there are no lovers here to have a quarrel, sir, I can assure you.
I would like to ask the hon. member how she squares her apparent distaste for certain elements in the arms trade now, with her party's enthusiastic endorsement of the development and testing of what everyone has agreed was in fact a destabilizing weapon that has come to be among the most terrible on the face of the planet.

Mr. Speaker, maybe the member did not hear the point I was making. The point I was making was the fact that while we get a very spirited condemnation of all sales of arms from the New Democratic Party, as articulated by the member opposite from Alberta, there has not been a member of the NDP from the province of Ontario who has opened his or her mouth to speak. The reason is because they are quite aware of the fact that the CAW very specifically has come out publicly in support of this particular legislation.
I am suggesting that we should put a realistic policy forward. Yes, for many years in Canada there have been arms sold and arms will continue to be sold as long as we live in a world where we are not neutral. We are not neutral at the moment and we need certain weapons of defence. But let us make sure that the control order put forth by the government specifies exactly to whom those arms are being sold and under what conditions. Those are the amendments that we are putting forward.
June 5, 1991

I do not like to have my colleague in the House stand up and decry the sale of all arms when his colleague in the riding in which they are selling the arms goes to his local union meeting and supports it. That is what I do not like and that is what I call hypocrisy.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make clear to my good friend from Hamilton East that I intend to speak next in this debate, unless the Conservatives are drawn into the debate. I want to raise a question with respect to that extraordinary final statement she made, which suggested that there were members of this House from the New Democratic Party who in fact had gone to labour councils-
You are going to be sorry, Steven.

If, in fact, any of my colleagues from the House have spoken out to local labour councils in favour of this piece of legislation, I would be very interested to hear the member provide evidence. If however there is no such evidence, I would expect the member to withdraw her statement.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, an NDPer is an NDPer. The member should be aware of the fact that the member from London Centre, a minister in his friend Bob Rae's government, has spoken in favour of the legislation, as well as another member of the NDP who is sitting in Queen's Park in Toronto. Clearly with the close ties that this member has with Bob Rae and his team at Queen's Park, I am sure he should know the position being taken by the cabinet of Bob Rae.

To make it clear, Mr. Speaker, on a supplementary question, there is of course no connection between the provincial government and its policies and the federal caucus of the New Democratic Party so far.
I put the question once more to the member. She has suggested that there are members of this caucus who have spoken in favour of this piece of legislation to labour councils. There is to my knowledge no such
