evidence any place in the province of Ontario. If she has evidence of members of this caucus having made such statements, I would ask her to document them to the House or else to withdraw a statement which clearly is not correct.

Mr. Speaker, I think if the hon. member reviews Hansard he will realize that I said NDP members. The last time I looked the minister from London Centre was an NDP member of the Legislative Assembly in the province of Ontario to which the member has associated himself on many occasions. I am sure he will reflect on the fact that at least two members of the NDP party-of which he is a member in the province of Ontario-now sitting in the Legislative Assembly at Queen's Park are in favour of this bill and speak in favour of it.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to follow my friend from Hamilton East who, as usual, has straddled the fence magnificently with respect to a difficult issue of principle. In other words, she made a speech which took the classic Liberal position of saying that: "If it is necessary to have legislation, well we would have better legislation than this but of course we would not want to give the impression that we were in favour of encouraging world arms trade", when in fact what this piece of legislation is about is precisely encouraging the world arms trade and perhaps most unfortunately, encouraging Canada's participation in that world arms trade.
I think that we should not have illusions or permit illusions to be put forward to people across this country about what this particular piece of legislation is about. It is not a piece of legislation which is designed, as the member for Hamilton East would suggest, to set up some kind of system of regulation, some system to let us see what is actually happening because we do not know what is actually happening. In fact, it is a piece of legislation which amends laws which already exist in this country, which prohibit the export of various weapons to countries around the world. It is not that we do not have, at the moment, ways of seeing to it that we have a record of what takes place with respect to imports and exports of arms. We have such records. What we do not have, up to this point, is the possibility of getting around those constraints as a country.

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
Perhaps the most telling part of this piece of legislation is clause 8. This particular clause amends the previous legislation which deals with imports and export permits. Let me just read from the present legislation:
Every one who imports, buys, sells, barters, gives, lends, transfers or delivers a prohibited weapon or any component or part designed exclusively for use in the manufacture or assembly of a prohibited weapon
(a)	is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years; or
(b)	is guilty of an offence punishable in summary conviction.
That is what the present law says. It prohibits certain weapons from being exported or delivered from this country.
What does this new piece of legislation do? It basically repeats that existing commitment, but then it adds to that which is described in this legislation as a saving provision, "Notwithstanding subsection (1)", which is the subsection that I just quoted. It continues:
-a person who carries on a business described in paragraph 105(l)(b) may export or import for a purpose that the Governor in Council prescribes by regulation to be an industrial purpose a prohibited weapon described in paragraph (c) or (e)- if that person does so under and in accordance with an export permit or an import permit, as the case may be, issued under the Export and Import Permits Act.
In short, what we have is the provision of a new loophole which makes it possible for the government to export what had previously been prohibited weapons under the present Import and Export Permits Act. That is at the heart of this legislation. It has nothing to do, as the member for Hamilton East suggested, with whether or not we produce arms in this country.
Of course, it is important for us in this country to continue to produce the arms of which our armed forces make use. Nobody in this party is suggesting that the arms which are produced for our armed forces should cease to be produced in this country. Nobody is suggesting that we should abolish the armed forces of Canada or that we should rely on imported weapons for those armed forces. Such nonsense.
The whole issue which the member for Hamilton East so successfully, unfortunately, tried to avoid is the question of whether we are going to permit prohibited weapons from being exported in the future. That is the issue. The Liberal Party is supporting this legislation, for what reason I cannot understand, but it is legislation which will have the effect of putting Canada in the centre of the world arms trade, as opposed to the not insignificant, but nevertheless fairly marginal position which we have had in that trade in the past.
The Liberal Party is in favour of us, as a country, being part, to a much greater extent, of the world arms trade and we in the New Democratic Party are proud to say that we are not in favour of that kind of expansion of Canada's participation in the world arms trade.
In my view, and I speak as a member from Ontario, as somebody from a constituency with many members from the Canadian Auto Workers, it would be a serious mistake for this country to move in that direction.
There are at least four reasons that I want to talk about that convince me that this would be a serious mistake. First, if we look at many of the Third World countries to which we provide billions of dollars of aid, which is often felt by many people in our country to be desperately needed here at home, but aid which is, nevertheless, provided by Canada and which we support providing, because it will help poor people in the Third World and give them some sense of hope for the future.
The reality is that much of that aid at the moment ends up providing foreign exchange to those Third World countries which is wasted on the build-up of huge armies, which is wasted on the destruction of neighbouring countries and which is wasted in civil wars. It just does not make sense for us as a country to, on the one hand, be providing help to Third World countries for water supplies, for housing and for food assistance and, on the other hand, to be increasing this world arms trade which is So destructive to many people and many regimes in Third World countries.
Second, our movement as a country into more involvement in the international arms trade contradicts completely the statements and commitments which this
June 5, 1991

government made in the aftermath of the Persian Gulf war.
Some of my colleagues have quoted from some of those commitments. I do not want to simply reproduce some of the government's statements, but I cannot help but point out what the previous minister of external affairs said on March 8. He said: "We cannot let a victory become a truce, an occasion for nations to re-arm, re-group and return to battle." For that reason, he suggested that there should be action to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the arms trade, the constant chase for spheres of influence.
This piece of legislation before us directly contradicts what the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested at that time in those statements. The Prime Minister was even more straightforward. He said: "We have all the technology in the world. We have all the resources we need. We could be big arms merchants. We chose not to be, although it is a very lucrative business. We have chosen not to be because it is fundamentally inconsistent with our policy to develop it, to peddle it, to finance it and then to deplore its use".
All I can hope is that members on the government side will listen this time to their Prime Minister. They will recognize that those words, which were said on March 13 by the Prime Minister of this country, require them to vote against a piece of legislation which takes us directly and deeply into the world arms trade.
I also want to point out that when we get into providing arms to Third World countries, arms to countries in the Middle East-and the suggestion here is that this is going to permit arms sales to Saudi Arabia-we open ourselves up to the possibility of providing arms that prop up regimes which often have human rights records which are absolutely deplorable.
Let me quote, for instance, from Amnesty International's report from 1990 with respect to Saudi Arabia. It says:
At least 27 prisoners of conscience were imprisoned and other prisoners of conscience may have been among more than 70 detainees held without charge or trial. Some political detainees were held without trial in prolonged incommunicado detention. Torture was reportedly common and one death in custody may have been caused by torture or ill-treatment. Sentences of amputation and flogging continued to be imposed and carried out. At least 111 persons were executed, 16 of them for political offences.
Government Orders
Those are the people to whom we are going to provide Canadian arms? That is shameful.
Finally, I want to point out, as a representative of an industrial constituency in Ontario, that in fact the money which is spent on the arms industry provides far less in the way of jobs than money which is spent in other sectors of our economy. For instance, a study which was done in the late 1970s indicated that at that time a billion dollars worth of spending on the military industry would create just under 45,000 jobs, while the same amount of money spent on the medicare industry, with respect to nurses, would create 85,000 jobs. That is almost twice as many.
That has changed even since that time in a way that has made the provision of money for the arms trade and for the military industry even less able to produce jobs than was the case in the late 1970s.
We have to begin to explore the conversion of our industries from arms production and arms export to the production of military related goods for our own country, yes, but more important to the production of industrial commodities and other commodities and services which serve our country and which serve people and people's needs rather than kill people and help to suppress human rights, as the comments with respect to Saudi Arabia indicate.
That is the direction we have to take. It is a direction which many countries in western Europe are taking. Companies in Britain and in other parts of western Europe have explored ways of converting their industries from arms production, military hardware and involvement in the international arms trade, to the production of items which are important to people's social and human needs.
That is the direction we must take in this country. It is not a direction which means that we intend to eliminate arms production for our Armed Forces. It is not a direction which is going to eliminate jobs in London or in Kitchener overnight. In that sense, it is not like the free trade deal, which has had such effects in London, in Kitchener, in Windsor and in hundreds of other communities throughout Ontario.
Instead, what we are looking for is an approach which will stop us from becoming part of the problem of the international arms trade, providing jobs for Canadians by meeting human needs instead of killing human beings.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION TO AUDIO TAPE STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Since there were no questions or comments. Debate.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-6, an act respecting the exporting, importing, manufacturing, buying or selling of or other dealing with certain weapons, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am naturally delighted to participate in this debate. I wanted to begin with a quote from the book of Isaiah regarding the changing of weapons into ploughshares. I will do that later if time permits.
June 5, 1991

I want to quote from a past President of the United States, Dwight D. Eisenhower. Many years ago he made the following comment: "Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired, signifies in this final scene, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed; those who are cold and are not clothed.
This world in arms is not spending money alone, it is spending the sweat of its labourers, the genius of its scientists, the houses of its children. This is not a way of life. Under the cloud of war, it is humanity hanging on a cross of iron".
What we are discussing today is nothing short of sinister. What we are discussing is really a complete reversal of what I think most Canadians believe to be one of the very fundamental theses of Canadian society, and that is that we are a peaceful country. We believe in peacekeeping. We believe in promoting peace in whatever way possible. This government is asking the House of Commons to permit Canada to enter the arms race in a serious way.
I think what we are being asked to do today is absolutely disgusting. I think it is absolutely incredible that the government is now taking this particular action after the comments of some of the critical spokespersons for the government. I want to quote from a speech made by the Prime Minister in this city on February 8, this year, referring to the gulf war: "One of the main lessons to be learned from the war is the danger to us all of the proliferation of both conventional and non-conventional weapons".
He went on to say:
"The major arms exporting firms and nations have contributed to the current crisis. The great majority of weapons in Iraq's arsenal came from suppliers in the countries of the five permanent members of the Security Council. This problem must be brought under control and the time to act is now".
We all thought the Prime Minister meant that the world would be moved to get out of the arms race, to start de-escalating the arms race. We thought that was what he meant. He went on to say: "When the war is over, the world community must co-operate to prevent the proliferation of these weapons and to roll back that proliferation which has already occurred".
The people of Canada thought the Prime Minister said that Canada ought to play some leadership role in the
Government Orders
de-escalation of the arms race. On February 20 of this year, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, and I quote from a speech that he made in London, England: "I believe it is imperative that the world declare that there be no Middle East arms bazaar. Ninety-five per cent of the weapons in the hands of Saddam Hussein came from the five permanent members of the Security Council". He goes on and on to say that Canada ought to be playing a leadership role.
Again, we thought the leadership role was to take Canada in positions in which we de-escalate. What we have is the spectacle, in spite of the comments of the Prime Minister of Canada and the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member from Alberta, of the government introducing legislation to encourage the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia.
Not hundreds of vehicles but nearly one thousand vehicles, mounted with automatic weapons, were negotiated on a government to government basis from the kingdom of Saudi Arabia to the Government of Canada to enable General Motors of Canada to get into the arms race in a major way.
Another deal is to encourage automatic weapons sales to the Netherlands. It goes on and on and on. If I had time I would read into the record pages and pages from this armaments book from Canada which lists all of the various technologies, all of the weapons that Canada produces for sale abroad. There is this sort of attitude on the part of most Canadians that Canada is not participating in this activity.
Year after year in the city of Ottawa we have the ARMX bazaar. This is the arms bazaar to which weapons' buyers come from all over the world to look at all the displays. I have been there myself and I could not believe what I was seeing. There were all kinds of machine guns, tanks, rocket systems, explosives, things that you can throw, things that you can shoot and it goes on and on and on. In other words, it is a whole bazaar of weapons of destruction sponsored and encouraged, in part, by the Canadian government. It happens right here in the capital city and arms merchants from around the world come here to shop.
At Suffield, Alberta, we have ongoing research into chemical warfare, but today while the government on one hand is bringing in legislation to restrict Canadian ownership of shotguns and rifles, it is bringing in legislation to encourage Canadian firms to get into the arms

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
exportation business. There is a certain element of conflict here and a certain element of hypocrisy.
When we listen to the statements by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs condemning the arms race and at the same time slipping in, via the other hand, legislation to encourage arms exports, it is no wonder the people of Canada wonder what on earth this government is up to.
Last year Canada's arms export was worth nearly $2 billion. This places Canada in the top 15 arms exporting countries of the world. I do not think Canadians know this. I do not think Canadians want to know this.
I know that the explanation by the minister, who sponsors this piece of peculiar and odd legislation, is that it will create jobs. I suppose, using that argument, we can get into the heroin business, we can get into the prostitution business and we can get into the drug dealing business. They all produce jobs, if that is the motive. Surely to goodness there is not a single member of Parliament who is not aware that a dollar invested in education, in construction of housing, in child care or in hospitals is a dollar that will create a lot more jobs than a dollar going into the arms industry. We all know that. If we want jobs, well then let us invest more into housing which Canadians need, and let us invest more into education and hospital care which Canadians need. If that is our motive we should be doing that.
The argument that we need this to create jobs is a bogus argument. If we permit this legislation, and this is why I oppose it so strongly as do all of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, then what is next? This is a sale of troop vehicles, with automatic weapons attached to them, to Saudi Arabia. All right, the kingdom of Saudi Arabia is going to get hundreds of these vehicles from Canada indirectly through the United States.
What else do we get into? In other words, what we are saying is that if this passes the door is open to get into the arms export business in whatever way Canadian firms wish.
I want to say that it was one of the saddest days of my life when we decided to discuss legislation here to privatize Canadian Arsenals. You remember that day, Mr. Speaker, you were here. We wanted a Crown
corporation in place to facilitate the development of military equipment and so on when Canada needed it.
It was a Crown corporation that permitted us in the threat of war or allowed us very quickly to mobilize an industry that could expand to fulfil and support Canada in its obligations. But when the threat of war was over and when the need was over, it could shrink up very quickly and those people could find jobs elsewhere. That was the theory of that Crown corporation.
It was in the ammunition business as well, and for us it made a lot of sense.
Now, of course, we have increasing numbers of private sector firms in the arms business. Their motive is one thing only: not the protection of Canada, not the protection of our sovereignty, but to maximize profits for their firms. That is the legitimate motive.
Once we get into that business of encouraging firms to get into the arms business, we are not just going to encourage them to keep expanding their businesses, which means expanding more and more into the arms production industry.
Is this what Canadians want? Is this the kind of country we want? No, it is not.
I see that my time is very limited. I simply want to say that we are speaking today on the principle of the bill. The principle is: Do we as a country wish to get into the arms export business? Do we as a country want to have legislation to facilitate private sector firms getting into the exporting of arms and weaponry throughout the world?
That is the question. That is the principle we are debating. I say no, we do not. I am extremely proud to say that the party with which I am associated says no, we do not want Canada to become a major arms player in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to another quote from the former President of the United States, as referred to by the previous speaker.
I would also like to congratulate the previous speaker on a very fine speech and for so succinctly assessing the situation as we found it.

President Eisenhower referred to one of the major threats to democracy, to the United States and to the freedom thereof. I am paraphrasing. We all know that he was referring to the military industrial complex.
I do not think there is anything to be gained by Canada in the expansion of the military industrial complex in this country as certainly this legislation would do. For that reason alone-a good enough reason and there are others-I stand here very proud to be opposing this legislation.
I guess it is impossible to address the matter of arms so soon after the conflict we have had in the gulf without somehow or another putting that conflict into the discussion.
I have a list here. There have been references made to the five permanent members of the Security Council of the United Nations having sold arms to Iraq, but there are others as well. I would be a bit repetitive in mentioning that the United States has sold weapons to Iraq. We are still referring to the gulf conflict.
Egypt sold weapons to the country of Iraq. Kuwait sold weapons to Iraq, as did China and the Soviet Union. Italy and Great Britain did the same. This is not an exhaustive list of those who sold, but the point is that certainly the United States, Egypt, and the United Kingdom were directly involved in the confrontation in the gulf.
If there is anything that can come out of the gulf that we should be grateful for, it is that the devastation of lives was not more extensive than it was. It was bad enough.
If you look at the state of Kuwait, one cannot help but notice that it suffered the greatest devastation of all outside the country of Iraq itself.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the joy-we can hardly call it that-which must today be felt by the citizens of Kuwait as they realize that they themselves helped to arm the very country which has wrought such destruction upon the country of Kuwait? To a greater or lesser extent that is the kind of situation which any country gets itself involved in whenever there is selling of arms.
There have been references made previously to Canada and the arms industry here. There have been references to what my party has said in relation to the
Government Orders
production of arms. I would like to reiterate, as one of the previous members of my party has already said, that of course there is no question Canada should not have Armed Forces. There is no question that the armaments for the most part and to whatever extent is possible, should be manufactured in Canada.
What we are saying is that we are not interested in expanding the military industrial complex in this country to the point where we are arming other nations and the very weapons we sell are used against us. Hopefully our peacekeeping capability and integrity will be restored.
The present legislation as it refers to the sale of arms from Canada is predicated on four different things: that there be no threat of selling arms from Canada to our allies; that we not sell arms to a country that is involved or is in imminent threat of becoming involved in hostilities, to a country that is under UN sanctions, or to a country where violations of human rights are occurring in any way.
I do not think there is any point in singling out Saudi Arabia, which happens to be the country most directly involved in this arms sale. I would not suggest for a moment that there is anyone here who would possibly believe an assurance that this legislation was brought in only for the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia. This legislation is just the opening of the door for the sale of Canadian arms, wherever possible the expanded military industrial complex can sell them.
I think in the immediate context it should be pointed out and reiterated that Saudi Arabia has been cited by Amnesty International. This is the same Amnesty International which the government quoted extensively, pointing out how vicious the Iraqi government was and using Amnesty International records to show that.
If we are going to stand in a debate in this House and cite Amnesty International in one context where hostilities are occurring, we have to do it in all cases.
I realize I only have 10 minutes to speak, but I would like to perhaps summarize a little bit later on. I only have two minutes left.
I have to point out now that Saudi Arabia has also been cited by Amnesty International for violations of human rights. This is something that I think should be emphasized as strongly as possible.

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
There are alternatives to the manufacture of arms. For years and years, if anyone cared to listen, such imaginative people, inventors, philosophers, whatever, such as Buckminster Fuller, have proposed alternate uses of the facilities for the production of destruction, ways to be able to turn them into peaceful uses.
There are alternatives.
For a member of the government to sit there and say that because we take this stand on this legislation that we are somehow calling the United Auto Workers murderers, for God's sake, is to lower the level of this debate to something which we on this side of the House have become accustomed to, I grant you, but certainly takes it to a lower level than we have ever had in a debate in this House before.
There are alternatives. I would suggest that rather than trying to sell more arms, what this country ought to be doing is showing leadership within the United Nations, where I would suggest we should be saying: "Listen, world, this situation has gone far too far; we have to start, for example, paying attention to what Amnesty International is saying". We should be saying to the world that we are willing to let the United Nations become involved in our internal affairs. That could be dangerous for us as well, but we should also be saying that if we are in a new world order, then the United Nations has to be able to become involved in the internal affairs of all nations. Perhaps we can do a lot toward eliminating the need for even the manufacture of arms itself.

Mr. Speaker, I am just trying to put my hands on the quotes from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I will do that in a minute.
I just want to make a few remarks on this bill. I am very interested in the issue of arms exports. I have been in this House of Commons some 12 years and I have constantly raised the issue of the transport of arms, especially to the Third World.
I raised the subject before in the context of "Irangate" where Trans-World Arms of Montreal was right in the thick of sending arms both to the Contras in Nicaragua and to Iran. Quite frankly, it was quite hard to get the
Canadian House of Commons or the Canadian media, and consequently the Canadian people, interested in this issue until the issue finally appeared in the American nightly news with Dan Rather, and when people found out that in Ollie North's safe in the White House there was evidence that a Canadian company was deeply involved in the illegal transport of arms.
It has been an issue that I am particularly interested in. I raised it again here in the House of Commons with respect to this particular deal, that is, the export of light armoured vehicles to Saudi Arabia, about an $800 million contract, and the other $100 million or so contract for the sale of guns, ammunition and so on to the Netherlands.
I had a press conference and no one came to it. No one seemed to be interested until the government brought forward a bill and now they are really interested. I think there has been some really interesting debate on this issue in the House of Commons.
It is not an easy question; it is a sad question, and it is a difficult question. It is easy to give rhetoric to it and one can shout about it from both sides, but I would just like to spend my short period here in this debate on a couple of points.
One of the points is a small but important point that was emphasized by the member for Kamloops a few minutes ago. That was the point of privatization. What happens when you privatize Canadian Arsenals, for example, and make it a private company? What can happen?. When we had a company like Canadian Arsenals, we could build it up when we needed it in the second world war or the Korean war and we could employ more people and make more guns and ammunition for the Canadian Armed Forces. Then, when we were a country at peace again, we could phase it down, because it was a matter of government policy. It was a Crown corporation and we could make other jobs for the workers. We could move them around to other jobs in the civil service or we could make sure they were looked after properly.
By and large, that worked. Once you privatized it, you got Diemaco of Kitchener. In order to survive, it has to go farther than the Canadian government contract for the armed forces and it has to export arms.
Once again, then, Canada becomes like many other countries in the business of exporting arms.
June 5, 1991

In a way, I have some sympathy. I will be frank and honest with General Motors in this particular contract. After all, it was the Department of External Affairs that went out and helped it get this contract with Saudi Arabia and promoted these contracts.
That seems to be the new role of External Affairs. It used to be that it was Canadian foreign policy. It used to be that it helped Canadian citizens when they were in trouble abroad or when they needed help as they went to a foreign country.
Now, its major role seems to be as a big trade department to promote sales of Canadian goods. Of course, one of the Canadian goods is arms. It leaves the government in contradictory situations making contradictory statements.
I was just examining the exchange in the House of Commons that I took part in on May 23 of this year. I cited the previous minister of external affairs, the right hon. Joe Clark. He said: "If there is one lesson which the world must learn from this war, it is that an unrestricted arms trade in this region, the Middle East, is no longer acceptable and constitutes a threat to the security of all members of the United Nations".
Of course, it looks contradictory to the average Canadian when the government then brings in this bill saying: "All right, let's export arms to the Middle East."
I asked this question of the Minister for International Trade in the House of Commons.
What did he say?

He tried to weasel out of it, quite frankly, by saying: "Mr. Clark meant restricted weapons".
Examine the phrase: "Unrestricted arms trade in this region". We are restricting the arms trade to this region. Who is he trying to kid? The fact is that the government has this contract. It has to change the law, and it is doing that.
It puts the government in a contradictory situation. The Prime Minister and the former minister of external affairs said: "Look, the Middle East is a dangerous area". There have been 26 wars since 1945 and there is only one peace treaty, which is between Israel and Egypt.
Everybody knows what kind of area it is and that there can be other wars there. The Prime Minister was right
Government Orders
and the minister of external affairs was right. Now, there is a contradiction here.
We cannot be holier than thou in this matter, and we should not pretend to be. Sweden has a socialist government. France has a socialist government. Name some other countries with socialist governments that export arms.
The late Rajiv Gandhi got into trouble when he was Prime Minister because of contracts with Sweden involving kickbacks and so on. This arms industry is a cancer in the world, and we have to blot it out. It takes political courage to do it.
One person who had some real political courage was the head of the machinists' union in the United States. He is now retired. His name was William Wimpensinger. They used to call him "Wimpy". He was no wimp, this man.
He went around to the machinists in the States and said: "I know we are going to lose some jobs if we cut back the arms industry, but by God, we have to do it or we are going to kill this world. We can find better jobs, brothers and sisters, outside the arms industry." That took political courage.
It is not easy for our party, quite frankly, to get up and oppose this bill.
I want to conclude by saying that it is easy to make a buck off arms, and we are starting to do that. However, we know that disarmament is tied into world development. Both of them are related. There are really two steps to the development of the Third World in the 21st century.
One is that the major powers give up making those weapons, and put some of that money into development. There is another aspect. This is where the Minister for International Trade missed again in the House of Commons when he said to me in his reply: "We were talking about weapons of mass destruction, and not about guns and light-armoured vehicles".
A weapon is a weapon is a weapon. If someone is killed by a bullet, they still are killed. If they are killed by a nuclear bomb, they are killed. If they are killed by a light-armoured vehicle and a bullet, whether in the townships of South Africa, in Central America or in the Middle East and so on, they still die.

June 5, 1991
Government Orders
More important, we keep sending these weapons- they are small weapons it could be argued-to Third World governments and governments throughout the world which use them on their own people, which use this kind of police force and this kind of anti-democratic system of government. This keeps down development.
There are two steps to development. One is eliminating the big weapons to have a peace dividend and the other is stopping the distribution of smaller weapons.
It would take political courage for a government to say we are not going to do it, we are not going to get into the international arms trade.
I sometimes think it might be nice to be an American congressman. They have a lot of power, a lot more power than we have as members of Parliament. Sometimes I really feel sorry for the American congressmen in many ways. They constantly have to defend weapons and defence contracts in their own constituencies and they cannot eliminate that cancer or oppose it. We are lucky here. We can oppose it. We can say to our union brothers and sisters: "Sorry, but the principle is more important. We can't get into this international arms trade".
The government is inconsistent. The government is wrong. It is so ironic that tomorrow we are going to debate gun control in Canada and today we are debating gun export to the world. It is wrong. It is simply wrong.
My friend, the member for Kamloops, was going to quote the Bible and I think he had to finish before he could do that. That is appropriate. In the past there have been numerous politicians from Kamloops who have been very good at quoting the Bible but he is right on this. The biblical quote was essentially the one about turning your swords into ploughshares.
One of the great times of my life was when as a young student I went to the United Nations for the first time and saw that great statue in front of the United Nations which is literally a picture of a sword being turned into a ploughshare. This government is not doing that. It is turning ploughshares into swords. That is shameful.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Taylor (The Battlefords-Meadow Lake) moved:
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Thai, in the opinion of this House, the government should establish a Bill of Environmental Rights to empower Canadians to fight polluters and guarantee all Canadians the right to live in a healthy environment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the importance of this motion to all Canadians could never be over-stated and it is most important that I am presenting this motion on World Environment Day during Environment Week, 1991.
Canadians from coast to coast to coast are all too aware that our environment teeters on the brink of irreparable destruction. Cynical attempts by governments to buffer big businesses' continued practice of sacrificing our land, our air and our water to cheap and

June 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
easy profits do nothing but sell off our childrens' right to a healthful future.
Tracts of forests one-third the size of Japan are sold to Japanese industry while our Prime Minister travels to that country and cosies up to their top big business executives to encourage more selling of our deteriorating forest. Our forest is shrinking. It is not being regenerated at the same rate that it is being removed. These forests are our lungs and home to countless disappearing species with which we share our country. We should be stewards of wild life, not executioners. Much of our disappearing forest will simply not be there for our children.
Water, air and land pollution continues to fume, spout and pour forth from industry and communities at an ever-increasing rate. Our fragile ecosystems cannot cope with the ravaging of violent toxins slathered across our environment. Government continues to support businesses' efforts to avoid often costly cleanups and environment impact studies of projects. Northern and remote residents, cottagers and tourists alike watch with frustration, shame and disbelief as acid rain continues to kill our lakes and rivers. The government's refusal to accept plans to phase in a long-term strategy of zero discharge for toxic effluents confound increasing attempts by individuals and communities to combat toxic biocide.
But our laws have not kept pace with the times. During the 1960s and 1970s, more and more Canadians raised their voices against environmental destruction and more and more of these people spoke with one voice. DDT, destruction of farm land and mercury poisoning were but a few of the key issues of the time. But our legal system still favours the polluter and environmentally hazardous developers over those who would give of their time and energy to protect, not to destroy, our environment.
Our citizens do not currently have the right to take sufficient action to protect the environment. The government's refusal to proceed with a serious environmental assessment bill serves only to underscore the unwillingness of cabinet to protect our nation's skin and tissue from pollution by eager developers who would sacrifice not only our environment but entire cultures, like the Cree facing the James Bay II project. The solution is no mystery. The collective expertise and experience of environmentalists and environmental organizations have produced reports which lay the basis for a very clear and effective environmental assessment bill,
but the government instead, turned the volume up on big business opposition to effective environmental assessment and refused to listen to what environmentalists had to say.
Our government may have the power to stop these acts, but as is the case, time after time after time, with Point Aconi, Kemano James Bay, Rafferty-Alameda and so on, our government has not the will or the backbone to listen to Canadians and put a stop to treating the environment like a sacrificial lamb on the altar of quick profit.
In fact, just last week the government had the opportunity to demonstrate a real commitment to the environment, but they chose not to do so.
All previous parliamentary business died when the House began a new session with a new throne speech on May 13. The government's then C-78 legislation, an act to establish an environmental assessment process had not passed and all testimony heard by the legislative committee studying that bill suggested that this was the best thing to happen to C-78, that it should have been put aside and the bill rewritten.
The government was given the opportunity to bring in new legislation which reflected an understanding of the need for a sound, well designed assessment process. But instead, they chose to reintroduce C-78, as if it had never died. C-78 is now C-13, a bad news number for a bad news bill. C-13 is the same old flawed and unsatisfactory bill that C-78 was, and it should not be that way.
The new Minister of the Environment had a golden opportunity to demonstrate that he had a real commitment to the environment and that he had listened to the experts on this bill. Instead, the new minister has taken up where the old minister left off and none of us are any better off. There is still no environmental assessment legislation in place in Canada.
I remain committed to developing a better assessment bill, and will continue to work to secure one for Canadians and their children who will inherit this mess that we are leaving behind.
The green plan had also presented the perfect window of opportunity to turn the comer away from continued escalation of pollution. But the government chose to turn this window of opportunity for positive change into a door to the trough for the friends of government. Green plan moneys are being squandered on pre-election ploys and we all lose because of it.
June 5, 1991

According to information gained through Freedom of Information requests, the federal government has spent more than $7 million on advertising-and public relations exercises around the green plan. To me, if the green plan was as good as the government says it is, no selling job would have been required, nor would the government have had to spend $12,000 on picture frames, $10,000 on lapel pins or $150,000 on communications advice from a private consulting firm.
Canadians already know that they want their government to work on the environment. The polls tell us that the environment rates high on Canadians' list of priority issues. Canadians are willing to support action on the environment. But $10,000 for lapel pins does nothing for the environment.
Obviously the sales job was not for the environment, it was for the Conservative party whose free trade agreement and goods and services tax have angered Canadians from coast to coast. Seven million dollars in taxpayers' money on the green plan should not have been directed for this clearly partisan purpose. The Tories should have used their own money in this shameful promotion.
It is equally shameful that we still have no measures to ensure that such a basic right as safe drinking water for all Canadians, a disgrace made absurd by the amount of fresh water available within our borders and made criminal due to the government's trade deal and the move to export more water to the United States industry, while so many Canadian citizens are denied fresh water to drink.
The current round of constitutional talks provides an opportunity to renew the values upon which our nation is founded, values of environmental respect and stewardship. I am proud that the leader of our party has called for an environmental accord to protect not only our resources, but our jobs as well. Any new constitutional accord must include a stronger recognition of environmental as well as social and economic rights.
What better measure to unite Canadians from coast to coast to coast? Polls and simple logic both show that our environment, the world in which we live, work and play, is a top priority for Canadians. This tremendous will to do something before it is too late should be harnessed to build a strong Canada. Pollution does not respect boundaries, it is a preventable disease which knows no borders.
Private Members' Business
A bill of rights would go a long way to dealing with these issues for many, many years to come. It would be central to the much needed integration of economic planning, social considerations and environmental protection. Instead the government continues daily to push changes which make environmental matters worse.
The Mexican trade deal is a case in point. Our government has mouthed the words of United States government and business by refusing to integrate environmental concerns into the trade negotiations. What shameful and backward thinking.
A bill of rights is the step that is needed to bring our laws into the last decade of the 20th century. A bill of rights would guarantee: "That people have the right to clean air, pure water and the preservation of natural, scenic, historical and aesthetic values of the environment."
Those words were from a private members' bill introduced some time ago by Ruth Grier, a member of the Ontario legislature and now the new Ontario Minister of the Environment. As minister, Ms. Grier has begun a process which will see the province of Ontario try to fill the gap created by this federal government as Ontario moves towards its own environmental bill of rights.
I have just returned from the Yukon where another NDP government, led by Premier Tony Penikett has introduced its own environmental bill. Here too we see that the territory is enshrining the right to a healthful, natural environment in their legislation and is therefore a leader among all legislators in this marvellous land we call Canada.
The federal government, in turn, has the obligation to conserve and maintain our environment for future generations. This is not a new idea. The Canadian Environmental Law Association has been pushing for an environmental bill of rights since at least 1970.
Any one person, or group of persons, who believe that a polluter is contaminating or degrading our environment, deserves the right to know the minister responsible will proceed in a serious way to determine the extent and nature of the problem, and be supported by legislation to give the government the power to stop, alter or otherwise change any existing or proposed project. Such a bill of rights would shift the burden of proof to the polluter, after establishing that environmental damage is the likely result of their action or their proposed project.

June 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
Such a bill of rights would give people the right to sue polluters, thrusting us finally into the role of nurturing stewards of our land. In this way we have much to learn from our indigenous people, who for so many years have tended and respected our environment.
It reminds me of a meeting this afternoon of the environment committee of this House where the Minister of the Environment told the members of the committee that he would like to see, through the green plan, the empowering of people on the environment. Nothing would empower the people more than a bill of rights. Such a bill of rights would ensure whistle blowing protection so that any worker has protection of the law in blowing the whistle on an employer who causes serious pollution, excessive waste of energy or deliberate or accidental contamination or degradation of our land, air or water. Workers deserve this right because not only will that go a long way toward preventing pollution at the source, but these workers who see big business pollution going on, know full well it is their children who will suffer from the effect of this environmental damage. Buyers and users of land have the right to be protected from buying polluted tracts of land, and consumers have the right to be able to choose and expect increasingly environmentally friendly products and packaging when there must be any packaging at all.
The people of our communities across this country deserve the right to sue the government and ensure that laws are enforced. There have been hundreds of cases in the United States where the Environmental Protection Agency has been sued on this basis. The majority of cases has been successful.
A bill of rights must also deal with the issue of compensation for workers who lose or must alter their livelihood because of essential environmental protection measures. Of course, workers through their organizations must be central to the decision-making process which concerns all dealings with the environment and particularly those which impact on industry and their jobs. Most importantly, all citizens must have the right to
be directly involved in this process through tribunals and panels.
Community based input is essential to ensure community based support for serious long-term environmental protection. People in communities deserve to be involved in all aspects of environmental decision making, the setting of standards and controls, the review of permits and regulations. They should receive adequate notice about all orders and regulations relating to control standards and public participation in decisions.
All members of this House should support this bill. Our environment is not something which we can leave until another time. There is no other time. Environmental organizations and community groups have made it all too clear to each and every member of Parliament in this House.
Today is the day to act. Today is the day to become a government with a commitment to the environment, a commitment to our children's future and our planet's future. Tomorrow is far, far too late.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, for introducing this bill which, I must say, I fully support.

I want to congratulate my colleague. He and I sat on the committee on Bill C-78 together. I know the environment is something he takes very much to heart. I support the bill. I support the initiative.
That being said, there are certain nuances that I would like to draw in the differences of opinion between him and me, and then there are certain fundamental differences which I would also like to bring to the attention of this House.
In terms of the nuances, the smaller differences, I do not believe that it was necessary in presenting this bill, which as he so properly said should involve all members of this House and indeed all of the Canadian people, for him to engage in a particularly blanket and vicious attack on Canadian entrepreneurs. It is not fair and it is not appropriate.
June 5, 1991

I am sure that if he were to review his remarks, he would really understand that it is not all business, not all of the private sector that engages in unlawful pollution. Yes, there are some businesses which do so and they should indeed suffer penalties. Let us not engage in universal condemnation.
At the same time I am sure that the member would want to recognize that there are other bodies who pollute, governments for instance, and municipalities that are not prepared to clean up their act. I am sure that the member, again if he were to go through his remarks, would not be so fulsome in his praise of the NDP government of Ontario. Indeed, the major environmental thrust in Ontario was due to the hon. James Bradley, the Liberal minister of the environment in that province. 1 am sure he would share again with me, if he were to review what he had said, the deep disappointment of the people of Ontario with the fact that the NDP government which did not expect to take power simply engaged in a lot of promises and has let the environmental community down very badly.
Let us go now to some of the more substantive differences of opinion between myself and this member, whom I admire greatly, and his legislation which indeed I ultimately support.
There is no doubt that the member for The Battle-fords-Meadow Lake is right when he says that the purpose of this legislation is to empower people to force governments to obey their laws.
He is also right when he examines the evolution of the EARP guidelines brought in by a federal Liberal government. Those guidelines, which were meant to bring polluters to heel by this unfortunate Conservative government, were simply regarded as guidelines. It has been successive court decisions which have forced the government to live up to its responsibility.
The member is right as well when he says that what is now happening is that we have guidelines that have the force of law. This government with C-78, now C-13, is attempting to bring in legislation which would only have the force of guidelines.
An environmental bill of rights is necessary to empower people.
Where I would disagree, with the member however, is how to empower people. It is not sufficient to only bring in an environmental bill of rights. That bill of rights must
Private Members' Business
have certain teeth. There are two suggestions that I would make to the member, within the context of the goodwill that exists and my support for his bill. The first is the absolute need for third party intervenor funding. It is not enough to simply empower people if, as a result of empowering them, we are ultimately going to bankrupt them as they begin the lengthy degree of court cases in an attempt to force government to live up to its own legislation.
Third party funding, which the current government has refused in the case of C-78, now C-13, on any kind of a reasonable level in virtually every court case, is essential if the Canadian people are to be allowed to expand democracy in the way that we all believe should happen. It would allow the Canadian people, not only to decide after the fact, but to have input into decisions as they are in the process of being made.
The second suggestion that I would make to the member in beefing up his bill is the necessity, within this House, of having an environmental auditor who would- and I have heard the member speak about this and he is nodding his agreement and we obviously share that view-have the same power as the Auditor General. He would report to Parliament whether the government was obeying its legislation and what progress the government had made on its commitment. He would be an environmental auditor who would really empower the people of Canada through their elected representatives.
I support the philosophy behind the member's bill and I would hope that this government would take the member's speech into account.

I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to ask the government, when it accepts the member's request which was so well formulated, to agree also to my suggestions regarding an environmental Auditor as well as third party intervenor funding. And I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to see the hon. member for lire Battlefords-Meadow Lake, give up his attacks against the private sector and not indulge in his desire which is quite understandable to praise the outdated NDP Ontario government.
I hope the government is really going to tackle the basic issues we are considering. I am sure, because I know the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment very well who is a man of high calibre and who shares our philosophy, that the government is going to accept these issues in an effort to really help the hon.

June 5, 1991

member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake win acceptance for his vision.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I am happy to participate in a debate and particularly a debate on the environment, like the one called for by the motion of the New Democratic Party.
This motion is asking the House to endorse the establishment by the government of a Bill of Environmental Rights. Such a Bill would give Canadians a chance to fight polluters and guarantee them the right to live in a healthy environment.
I must state, Mr. Speaker, that protection of the environment and improvement of its quality are amongst the top priorities of this government. Our track record clearly shows to what extent we are determined to work to that end. On December 11, 1990, we made public our environment action plan entitled "Canada's Green Plan". The basic principle of this plan is shared by all Canadians: To guarantee to the present and future generations a healthy and safe environment and a strong and thriving economy. The best way to guarantee to the citizens of this country a clean environment is to set ourselves very definite goals and keep people abreast of the progress we are making toward them. This, Mr. Speaker, is the essence of the Green Plan. It contains specific objectives and timetables. It provides for regular consultations and detailed reporting on the environment, to allow the public to follow closely the progress being made.
Mr. Speaker, the commitment made by the government to improve the environment will be enshrined in the legislation. The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, which establishes the federal environmental assessment process, states, in its preamble, that the government seeks to achieve an appropriate balance between economic development and the preservation and enhancement of environmental quality.
Mr. Speaker, impact studies were done in my riding concerning the completion of highway 50 between La-chute and Mirabel. Of course, these studies have held up for quite some time, the construction of that highway which is necessary, if not essential to the development of the large region of Argenteuil. And I can tell you that the people of my riding were very aware of the quality of
the environment. They, of course, wanted to preserve the environment, but not by having to go through red tape and additional delays. The latter are often welcomed by the government's financing the construction of those highways, who end up making commitments over several years, but which in fact are detrimental to regional development. A balance must therefore be found and I certainly agree with the government's objective of achieving an appropriate balance between economic development and the environment.
That bill also provides that all departments and federal agencies must make an environmental assessment for all the projects concerning which they have a decision making power. The legislation also gives far reaching powers to the Minister of Environment, so that he can ensure that the process is applied fairly, efficiently and openly. Moreover, and this is a very important aspect, those powers will ensure that the public can contribute to a large extent to the decision making process regarding projects which may have serious consequences on the environment.
Over and beyond this legislation, the Prime Minister has pledged unequivocally, on behalf of the government, that the environment would be a priority in all the decisions concerning policies and programs. Mr. Speaker, the government realizes that the Prime Minister's actions have a bearing on the life of the Canadian population in ways that are not always directly linked to his projects. That is why the government now requires that policy and program proposals submitted to Cabinet which may have a substantial impact on Canada's environment, must be accompanied by a statement of their environmental impact.
Thanks to the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act and the policies of the Canadian government, almost every important measure contemplated by the government will be examined from the environmental perspective. Canadians will have the right to be directly involved in the process or at least have access to the results.
The Minister of the Environment is responsible for implementing the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. This legislation confers very broad powers on the minister for issuing regulations to protect air, water and soil quality in Canada. Furthermore, the legislation requires the minister to report regularly to Canadians on the state of the Canadian environment.
June 5, 1991

Thanks to this legislation, the public can be actively involved in decisions that have an environmental impact. The legislation also gives the public the might to prosecute polluters who violate the Act.
The government is also very much aware of the importance of providing information on the environment, Mr. Speaker. In the course of consultations with Canadians as the government was developing its Green Plan, it was often said that the government should set a very high priority on regular dissemination, on a broad scale, of easily understood information on the state of the environment and any changes that have been corded.
Canadians also told us, Mr. Speaker, that they wanted to be able to base their environmental decisions on solid ground. They wanted good, solid information to determine whether their individual actions would help reduce the deterioration of the environment. They also wanted to be able to judge whether the government was also doing its share to leave a healthy and sustainable environment for future generations, and to be able to make an informed assessment of the performance of industry with respect to the environment.
To provide regularly quality information on the environment is one of the principal commitments made in the Green Plan. Although much remains to be done in this very complex field, the government is committed to providing Canadians with the information they need to make enlightened decisions regarding their own activities and those of others-including governments and industry-as they affect the quality of the environment.
I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the government feels that the steps we have already taken are indeed the best way for the Canadian people to fight polluters and for the government to fulfill its commitments. We have already taken the necessary steps to ensure that all Canadians have the right to live in a healthy environment. I think this Bill of Environmental Rights would duplicate many existing provisions. It would be better to let the voters concerned about the environment be the judge of the government's performance. That is true
Private Members' Business
accountability! The Canadian people will decide if we have not achieved our goals regarding the environment.
In my riding as in others, Mr. Speaker, I think that most of the people involved and active in local environmental associations know very well that, while working towards a healthy and sustainable environment, they have to bear in mind that economic development must go on. We cannot stop the march of time unduly and prevent the implementation of an industrial project designed to provide employment for fear that a bee will not be gathering nectar.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I hope that my constituents will take part in the green plan implementation process. There will be programs to encourage participation in special projects. Being a member yourself, you know very well, Mr. Speaker, that people interested in doing various things, be it recycling bottles, newspapers, whatever, are coming to see us regularly in our ridings. For years now, one of my constituents has been wishing that the government would come up with a little program to finance the purchase of a vehicle, allowing him to expand his business and gather more cardboard for recycling and resale to companies prepared to buy it from him.
So, I am convinced that the green plan will give my constituents the opportunity, or so I wish, to be more directly involved in the protection of our environment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to take part in this debate and support the motion moved by my colleague, who calls for the government to establish a Bill of Environmental Rights to empower Canadians to fight polluters.
I listened carefully to what the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau had to say. Of course, she praised the green plan introduced by her government, but, at the same time, she opposed the motion before the House asking the government to establish a Bill of Environmen-

tal Rights to empower Canadians to fight polluters and everyone who is destroying our country's environment.

Let us assume, for instance, that this government is totally incompetent. I know it is not beyond possibility, but we on this side of the House will help the government to produce such legislation.
My colleague from LaSalle-Emard would be more than pleased I am sure to assist the government and the parliamentary secretary in preparing the kind of legislation that we need in the event that the government is as incompetent as some of the Tories across the way think it is.
The Tories were talking about the green plan. I can think of two reasons why it is called the green plan: the environment is green, and it is a green slush fund. The only thing green is the money coming into the government advertising agencies which are benefiting from the green plan.
