speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address the House on what is a very interesting proposal, one for which I am afraid there may be excessive expectations. Those are the kinds of issues which I would like to address during the next few minutes.
All members of this House irrespective of party share a very common and strong desire to protect the environment. As a result of an enhanced amount of environmental awareness over the last perhaps five to ten years, I think there is a widespread realization not only in this
June 5. 1991

House but throughout the country that Canada's environment, the environment of other nations, and indeed the global environment is very much under attack.
While some individual members may have led in the forefront in their efforts in this House to increase awareness, I think it is true to say that at this time there is not a single member in the House who is not in broad agreement that an immense amount of work needs to be done in order to undo many of the mistakes of the past.
A question which is uppermost in my mind is how we should go about addressing what is obviously a very monumental problem, a problem which faces us as a federal government, a problem which faces each of the provincial governments throughout the country, a problem which faces the municipal governments as well, faces us as individuals and within the international community.
At first blush the thought of an environmental bill of rights is certainly an attractive one, and I would congratulate the hon. member for making sure that it is a point of debate in this House. I would encourage him to continue with a suggestion that even if he is not successful on this particular occasion, it may well be that the idea with the passage of time will develop to the point of a broader degree of understanding.
It seems to me that what we must address right now is the question of what we would expect of an environmental bill of rights and how we would best go about achieving those several objectives. I believe what we are looking for as Canadians and as parliamentarians is some sort of assurance that the various levels of government will work together among themselves, with the environmental groups, with the business community, and with citizens at large in order to ensure there is a broad framework in place to try and protect the environment in the future from some of the ravages of the past.
I see this broad framework including many facets. I see it including federal legislation. I think of the Canadian Environment Protection Act which is already law. I see it including many regulations, many of which will emanate from that Canadian Environment Protection Act, and I am veiy conscious in my responsibilities as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment that we still have a significant distance to go in the establishment of those regulations.
Private Members' Business
As I say that, I am also conscious that government alone will not accomplish a great deal if it simply passes regulations without working in close consultation with other jurisdictions of government and with those whose actions should be regulated. Very often that is, but not solely, the business community, the industrial community. Of course individuals must be a part of that process as well.
I believe that the provincial governments' jurisdictions must be a part of this process, part of this multi-faceted approach to achieve the over-all objective which we are pursuing. I am very conscious of the constitutional fact that the provincial governments are largely responsible for the control of natural resources within the Confederation of Canada. To be frank, many provincial governments today are fearful that the federal government either is or may be on the verge of intruding upon what it perceives to be its jurisdiction.
In my own mind I am very clear on the fact that I believe Canadians are asking this federal government to accept a major role of leadership and I believe it is appropriate it should do so. But I also believe it will be more effective if we can work in co-operation with the provinces rather than confrontation with the provinces. They are a very important part of the multi-facet approach.
I would like to say that I believe the NGOs, the environmental non-governmental organizations, have a major role to play in this process. To me they bring a wealth of experience, a vast amount of knowledge and as well some very obvious, sincere convictions on the need for the environment to be protected. I see them as partners in the process, just as I do individuals who are becoming increasingly conscious of the need to protect the environment.
I spoke once before in this House about an individual constituent who wrote to me some time ago. I would like to remind the House of that one single letter because the message, I thought, was so meaningful, somewhat symtomatic of what I see happening in Canada. She was an older woman, according to her letter, living alone in a very small community within my constituency of Brandon-Souris. She wrote to say that she was concerned about the manner in which she was heating her house and whether or not in using the fuel oil which was available to her she was in any way endangering the

June 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
environment. She sought advice as to what she should do as a result of that.
I was very touched by that letter because here was evidence of an individual Canadian, perhaps without substantial monetary means, who was clearly prepared to make some sort of sacrifice in order to do her part in what she perceived to be a Canadian struggle in order to protect the environment.
I guess what impressed me about that particular letter was that she wrote out of a genuine sense of concern and conviction. She did not write as a result of regulations requiring her to do so. She did not write because of a particular piece of legislation on which she based her concerns. She wrote as an individual who had grown aware of certain dangers and she was willing to do her part and respond.
I think what I see right now in this country, and elsewhere in the world, is a tremendous need for the development of partnerships in which all people will understand-perhaps to say all would be naive-but a vast majority of Canadians and citizens throughout the world would understand that we have a common responsibility to address the problems which face us in a co-operative and partnership manner.
One of the reasons why I am hesitant to see an environmental bill of rights as being some sort of solution to the challenge which is before us right now is that I fear it would suggest that somehow or other we could depend upon a particular piece of legislation, and the courts, which would presumably be an important partner in the process, to absolve ourselves of any other responsibilities and to be some sort of panacea in itself.
I accept the fact that legislation and courts may be an essential part of the over-all process of protecting the environment. I am sometimes as frustrated as other members are when I see that sentences levied against polluters are not as severe as I would wish them to be. I really believe that the best guarantee for a safe environmental future lies in a widespread determination to accept our responsibilities as individuals and whatever level of government we may be a part of, or whatever role we play in society, rather than put all of our hopes in
a single piece of legislation or in the courts and ask them to enforce them.
We must work together and by working together we can succeed.
I was struck during the course of the green plan consultations how many hundreds, indeed thousands of Canadians who came forth, even though they came with a great deal of scepticism at the start, willing to be a part of the process. I would suggest that it is out of that sort of search for solutions that will come the strategies of tomorrow.
It may well be some time into the future that the environmental bill of rights will fit in perhaps to a multi-faceted approach as the hon. member wishes, but I believe right now the priority of this government, other governments and Canadians wherever they may be, whether individually or collectively, should be in trying to form the kind of partnerships the green plan is addressing.
While I congratulate the hon. member for ensuring that this issue is very much an issue to be debated now and again in the future, I would suggest perhaps that there are other issues and other solutions that are more important at this point in time. I look forward to that debate continuing on into the future.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to talk to the member's motion. The motion, as others have said, would have the government consider the creation of an environmental bill of rights to empower Canadians-and I think we should remember those two words clearly, empower Canadians-to fight polluters and guarantee all Canadians the right to live in a healthy environment.
I am sure veiy few of us would quarrel with the member's objectives on this issue. Certainly I would not and I know few people in my constituency would quarrel with that concept. We want a clean, healthy and productive environment for ourselves, for our children and certainly for future generations.
Let us not choose a means of questionable effectiveness to achieve an end which we can all support. The creation of an environmental bill of rights is an appealing
June 5, 1991

notion, but is it in reality the best way to achieve the
goals?
I would like to reflect just for a moment on our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Certainly it provides Canadians with individual rights beyond those of most nations. Many people of the world would consider our Charter of Rights and Freedoms a model for their countries. Yet sometimes, when it is taken to an extreme, one really wonders if, in certain aspects, it is in the best public interest.
I will give an example of one of those extremes, what I think of as an extreme. I look at the situation of criminals in this country who are here claiming refugee status to evade punishment in other countries. I see how they use our laws, or maybe I should say abuse our laws, and I wonder whether this is in the best public interest of Canadians in general.
Sometimes one wonders if we have not taken individual rights a step too far in certain situations. Sometimes I wonder, when I think of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, if we should not have brought along a charter of responsibility, or maybe a charter of responsibility and opportunity to go along with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In drafting an environmental bill, again I am going to purposely use an extreme, one might very well draft around the sort of issue that I am going to bring up. Certainly one can look at the automobile. The automobile certainly pollutes the atmosphere. If a bill of rights for the environment were drafted in a fairly broad way, an individual could bring action against neighbours and against the public in general on the use of the automobile, a polluting device in our environment. Could the banning of the automobile result from that sort of action?
Again, that is an extreme, but certainly one has to be careful when one looks at what exactly pollution is and how it affects us as individuals.
I did not mean to be partisan in this talk today. The opposition took a few definite shots. I suppose one should reflect on the situation and I suppose, to a certain extent, I will be partisan in my next couple of comments.
I used to be a member of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario. It was interesting that during my years there, two members of the Liberal party had Private Members' Bills-actual bills, not just motions-suggesting that the government bring forward a bill of environmental rights. Interestingly enough, both of those members ended up
Private Members ' Business
in the Liberal cabinet later in the 1980s and neither one of them ever brought forward a bill of rights for the environment.
Subsequently, just a year or two later, the NDP critic for the environment brought in a Private Members' Bill almost identical to the bills that the two members I referred to previously had introduced to the Ontario legislature. Once again, now that the NDP is in power its promise of a bill of rights on the environment is at least delayed, and quite possibly we will not see it forthcoming.
Again, I think the problem is that while the concept is good and everybody generally supports the idea and individuals want more power to deal with environmental issues, when it comes to actually writing a bill, it is rather difficult to word it in a proper way so that it is not taken to an extreme.
Therefore, let us look at some of the possibilities of empowering people, giving them more ability to react and help in the improvement of our environment.
I am not going to talk at great length about the green plan because other members have done so. Certainly, the green plan is based on a vision which all Canadians will share in. When one looks at the individual programs in the green plan, a few of which have been announced and many more will be announced over the next six years, there are many areas where individual Canadians can take a very active involvement.
Just to briefly mention two. There can be individual attempts to reduce solid waste-whether by a family or a business-through recycling, judicious purchasing and reducing the amount of packaging in the products we purchase and the use of composting. There are a great many areas where an individual can take action, and very distinct action, to assist in saving our environment.
Another opportunity to assist in the environment is the community tree planting program. That will be announced soon, I hope. That will allow individual Canadians and local organizations to get very much involved in planting trees across Canada.
The other piece of legislation I had hoped to talk about is the Environmental Assessment Act but I see my time is rather limited. There certainly will be opportunities for Canadians to be involved in that. The one I wish to mention at the end is the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. That gives extensive rights to public participation and decision making affecting the environment. It also confers upon the public the power to take

June 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
court action when an activity contravenes the act. I think, to a significant degree, the empowerment within the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, and the new assessment act when it passes, will go a long way toward giving individual Canadians the thrust that they wish to have to improve our environment.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR BILL OF ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take the couple of minutes I have remaining to say a few words about Motion M-217 brought forward by my colleague from Saskatchewan.
The hon. member's riding is just west of where my riding is in western Manitoba. When you speak of the environment, if you come out to my part of Manitoba you can look up and see the clear blue sky, and about 300 yards away from my home in Swan River, Manitoba you see nature at its best. We have small mountain ranges with the grass and trees growing. People in the urban centres of Canada cannot appreciate the type of environment that we are able to live in. But, of course, if things keep going the way they have been going over the recent past, that is very much at risk.
I will give one example specific to my part of Manitoba. Back in 1989 the Repap Corporation purchased a
large pulp mill in La Pas, Manitoba, and in doing so acquired the cutting rights to a major portion of Manitoba, including the area around where I live in Swan River. Included in the purchase were plans of major expansions, both in La Pas and a chipping plant in Swan River. They had planned to follow up on several other areas. What has come to pass since that time is that Repap is subject to several environmental studies to enable the corporation to expand. So even in the pristine part of Manitoba and areas in western Canada, the governments and citizens involved are very very sensitive to the environment and are making sure that these projects are subject to environmental studies before they go forward.
